chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Capstone Energy+ emerged from a compressed but consequential corporate metamorphosis. Founded in 1988 in Van Nuys, California as Capstone Turbine Corporation, the company spent three decades commercialising the microturbine before renaming itself Capstone Green Energy Holdings in 2021 to signal a pivot toward integrated microgrid contracting. That pivot proved insufficient to arrest a liquidity spiral: on September 28, 2023, Capstone Green Energy filed for Chapter 11 in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware in a pre-packaged restructuring, with Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group as the dominant pre-petition creditor. The company emerged on December 7, 2023 with a restructured balance sheet and new ownership. On May 15, 2026 — eight days before this dossier's snapshot date — the company completed its final identity shift, legally renaming itself Capstone Energy+, Inc. Its OTCQX ticker, CGEH, remained unchanged. The OTCQX listing reflects the reduced disclosure cadence appropriate to a post-emergence entity: public filings arrive materially less frequently than those of a NASDAQ-listed peer, and disclosure gaps are noted throughout this dossier where they constrain analysis.

## Core Business

Capstone designs, manufactures, and services microturbine systems spanning 30 kilowatts (C30) through 1.2 megawatts (C1200S), with packaged multi-unit configurations reaching several megawatts of on-site generating capacity. The machines burn natural gas, biogas, propane, and flare gas with lower NOx emissions than reciprocating engine alternatives and no oil-lubricated components, yielding lower service intervals. Post-emergence strategy has emphasised Energy-as-a-Service: power purchase agreements, energy service agreements, and long-term equipment rentals that convert capital-equipment sales into multi-year contracted revenue. In fiscal 2025, the rental and EaaS segment contributed $14.4 million — 17 percent of total revenue — establishing a recurring baseline that did not exist at the same scale before the restructuring. [FY2025 Press Release](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/4040/)

Customer applications span oil and gas flare-gas utilisation at upstream well sites (the largest single application category), industrial combined heat and power for food and agricultural manufacturing, district energy for university campuses and hospital complexes, hospitality cogeneration, and — emerging — AI data centre backup and bridge power. The company had deployed more than 10,600 units across 88 countries as of the May 2026 rebrand announcement.

## Revenue and Financial Posture

Pre-Chapter-11 revenue stood at approximately $77 million in fiscal 2023 (ended March 31, 2023). The restructuring year — fiscal 2024 — produced $91.2 million as order activity pulled forward ahead of the filing. Fiscal 2025 revenue declined to $85.6 million, partly on European market hesitancy during the post-emergence transition, but the year produced Capstone's first-ever positive full-year adjusted EBITDA of $7.9 million. In the nine months ended December 31, 2025, revenue reached $83.0 million, up 42 percent year-over-year, with trailing twelve-month revenue of approximately $110 million. [Q3 FY2026 Results](https://ir.capstoneenergyplus.com/press-releases/detail/4064)

| Period | Revenue | Adj. EBITDA |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 (pre-filing) | ~$77M | n/a |
| FY2024 (emergence year) | $91.2M | n/a |
| FY2025 | $85.6M | +$7.9M |
| TTM through Dec 2025 | ~$110M | — |

Cash at March 31, 2025 stood at $8.7 million against total liabilities of $82.6 million, producing a stockholders' deficiency of $21.6 million — a balance sheet consistent with a company still digesting its emergence. That posture shifted materially when Monarch Alternative Capital closed a $112.5 million strategic investment on March 31, 2026: $80 million in senior convertible preferred stock, $15 million in common equity, and a $17.5 million concurrent PIPE. Proceeds fully redeemed Goldman Sachs's legacy preferred position, extinguishing the dominant structural liability of the post-emergence balance sheet. [Monarch Investment Close](https://ir.capstoneenergyplus.com/press-releases/detail/4066) Post-Monarch balance sheet data was not yet public within the snapshot window; Q4 FY2026 earnings were scheduled for June 25, 2026.

## Leadership and Market Position

Vincent J. Canino was appointed President and CEO on March 11, 2024, three months after emergence, succeeding Robert Flexon who held the interim role through the restructuring. Canino brought thirty years of energy-sector experience including the chief operating officer role at long-duration storage company ESS Tech (NYSE: GWH) and the president and CEO role at Smardt Chiller Group. John P. Miller assumed the Interim CFO role in November 2025. As of May 22, 2026, CGEH traded at approximately $10.02 per share, implying a market capitalisation of roughly $304 million on approximately 30.3 million shares outstanding — a 52-week range of $0.31 to $13.80 that captures the full arc of the post-restructuring equity discovery process. [StockAnalysis](https://stockanalysis.com/quote/otc/CGEH/)

The AI data centre narrative, while prominent in post-emergence investor communications, remained at the framework stage within the snapshot window. A memorandum of understanding with Microgrids 4 AI (MG4AI) in September 2025 and an 800-volt direct-current microturbine architecture announcement in October 2025 established the technology positioning; no revenue-generating customer contracts had been publicly disclosed as of May 23, 2026. [MG4AI MOU](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/4048/)

## The Central Question

Capstone Energy+ enters its post-restructuring growth phase with a cleaner balance sheet following the Monarch transaction, a revenue trajectory approaching $110 million on a trailing basis, and a commitment — as part of the Monarch terms — to pursue a national exchange listing within twelve months of the March 2026 close. The dossier asks the harder questions: what does the restructured cap table actually deliver to equity holders once Monarch's convertible preferred is layered in, how durable is the EaaS revenue conversion against Bloom Energy, Cummins, Caterpillar, and distributed gas-generation alternatives, and what does AI data centre bridge-power demand require that Capstone's microturbine architecture can credibly supply at commercial scale?

chapters.title: From 1988 Capstone Turbine through Green Energy rebrand to Chapter 11 and Energy+
chapters.body:
## Origins: The 1988 Founding and the Promise of Distributed Generation

The company that would eventually emerge from Chapter 11 bankruptcy as Capstone Energy+ traces its origins to 1988, when engineers in Van Nuys, California began developing what they believed would be a transformative technology in distributed power generation: the microturbine. Unlike conventional reciprocating gas engines, the microturbine concept promised a single moving part rotating on air bearings that required no lubricating oil, ultra-low emissions from a recuperated combustion cycle, and the ability to run on a wide variety of gaseous fuels — from pipeline natural gas to landfill methane to flared associated gas at upstream oil-and-gas well sites.

Capstone Turbine Corporation spent the 1990s refining the technology through iterative product development, accumulating intellectual property, and cultivating early adopters in the oil-and-gas and industrial cogeneration segments. The C30 — a 30-kilowatt unit compact enough to fit inside a standard enclosure — was its initial commercial offering, designed for applications where grid power was expensive, unreliable, or unavailable. By the late 1990s, the company had working hardware, a growing installed base across multiple geographies and customer categories, and enough commercial traction to attract capital-market interest during what would prove to be an extraordinarily forgiving moment for technology companies of any description.

## The 2000 NASDAQ Listing and the Accumulating Deficit

Capstone Turbine Corporation went public on NASDAQ in 2000, raising capital in a market simultaneously beginning to price in a very different kind of future. The listing positioned Capstone as a clean-energy technology company at the intersection of distributed generation and low-emissions power — a story that resonated with the emerging green technology narrative even before "ESG" had become standard institutional vocabulary.

What followed was a multi-decade exercise in sustaining a commercially viable product against a backdrop of chronic operating losses. Fiscal year after fiscal year, Capstone reported revenues that demonstrated genuine market demand — customers in oil and gas, industrial cogeneration, district energy, hotel combined heat and power, and related segments were buying and deploying microturbines — while also reporting operating losses that accumulated into a nine-figure cumulative deficit. The microturbine technology worked. The business model did not close.

| Fiscal Year (ending March) | Revenue (USD millions) |
|---|---|
| FY2020 | $75 |
| FY2021 | $73 |
| FY2022 | $95 |
| FY2023 | $77 |

*Source: Capstone Green Energy NASDAQ-era SEC filings, as summarised in company financial disclosures.*

Revenue fluctuated within a comparatively narrow band across multiple fiscal years without translating into sustained profitability. The underlying challenge was structural: microturbines occupy a specific niche in distributed power, competing with reciprocating gas generators on emissions and fuel flexibility but carrying higher upfront capital costs that demand longer payback periods. Converting that niche appeal into the scale required to absorb a public company's sales infrastructure, product development overhead, and service organisation proved persistently difficult. By the early 2020s, the company had spent more than two decades publicly listed on NASDAQ without demonstrating a durable pathway to positive operating income. Accumulated deficit disclosures in the company's SEC filings had grown to exceed $1 billion.

Yet the product line had continued to mature in parallel. The C30 had been joined by C65, C200S, C600S, C800S, and C1000S signature-series configurations, and eventually by the C1200S at 1.2 megawatts — enabling packaged multi-unit microgrid systems capable of delivering several megawatts of dispatchable power from a single coordinated installation. The technology was not stagnant; the commercial model was the constraint.

## 2021: Capstone Green Energy and the EaaS Pivot

Against a backdrop of accelerating ESG capital allocation and growing institutional interest in energy-transition narratives, management executed the company's first corporate rename in 2021. Capstone Turbine Corporation became Capstone Green Energy Corporation — a rebranding positioned not merely as a marketing exercise but as a signal of strategic direction.

The pivot was toward Energy-as-a-Service. Rather than selling microturbine hardware and collecting a product margin, the company would structure integrated microgrid contracts under which customers paid a recurring service fee in exchange for on-site dispatchable power, heat recovery, and ongoing asset management — with Capstone owning or co-financing the underlying equipment. The EaaS model promised more predictable recurring revenue, deeper long-term customer relationships, and a valuation framework more consistent with infrastructure-service multiples than conventional industrial equipment sales.

The rationale was coherent. The execution challenge was financing. Converting a capital-light hardware-sale model into a capital-intensive equipment-ownership model requires balance-sheet capacity that Capstone Green Energy did not possess in abundance. Service contract origination demands working capital to deploy assets ahead of recurring revenue recognition. For a company carrying a persistent operating deficit and constrained access to investment-grade debt markets, the EaaS transition demanded bridge financing that would prove increasingly difficult to sustain as the macro environment shifted.

## September 28, 2023: Chapter 11 in the District of Delaware

On September 28, 2023, Capstone Green Energy Holdings, Inc. filed for Chapter 11 protection in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. The filing had been structured in advance as a prepackaged plan — the company had negotiated the terms of its restructuring with its principal secured creditor, Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group, before appearing in court, with the specific intention of confirming a reorganisation plan and emerging from Chapter 11 on a compressed timeline.

The precipitating factors, as reflected in court filings and contemporaneous public disclosure, included liquidity tightening across a rising-rate macroeconomic environment that had compressed working capital availability across leveraged industrial businesses, customer-receivable concerns that created cash-conversion stress, and the operational scaling challenges inherent in pivoting an asset-light hardware business toward an equipment-ownership EaaS model. The pre-petition balance sheet carried secured debt obligations to Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending that the company could not service on an ongoing basis.

Long-tenured chief executive Darren Jamison, who had led the company through the 2021 Green Energy rebrand and the EaaS strategic pivot, departed as the restructuring process unfolded. The prepackaged structure itself reflected the relative concentration of the creditor group: Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending held the dominant secured position, enabling bilateral negotiation of plan terms before the court filing rather than the protracted multi-party negotiations that characterise contested Chapter 11 proceedings. A prepackaged confirmation compresses the bankruptcy timeline dramatically, reducing the value destruction — customer attrition, management distraction, vendor credit tightening — that accumulates during extended court-supervised reorganisations.

## December 7, 2023: Emergence and the Capstone Energy+ Rebrand

Capstone Green Energy emerged from Chapter 11 on December 7, 2023 — approximately ten weeks after the filing date, a compressed timeline consistent with the prepackaged structure's design. The emergence was the product of a confirmed plan of reorganisation that converted the secured debt held by Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group and other pre-petition creditors into reorganised equity in the restructured entity. Pre-Chapter-11 common shareholders — holders of the NASDAQ-listed equity — were substantially wiped out, consistent with the standard priority waterfall in a prepackaged restructuring where secured creditor claims exceeded enterprise value available to junior interests.

The post-emergence company — now trading on OTCQX under the ticker CGEH, a material step down in listing tier from its NASDAQ predecessor — subsequently rebranded as Capstone Energy+, Inc. The name change shed the "Green Energy" framing that had defined the 2021-to-2023 chapter and adopted a posture more explicitly oriented toward reliable, dispatchable power delivery. Post-emergence financial disclosure cadence reflects the OTCQX reporting standard, materially less granular than the SEC-reporting cadence of the NASDAQ predecessor; investors should treat post-emergence financial detail as a disclosure gap relative to what the pre-Chapter-11 entity provided through quarterly 10-Q and annual 10-K filings.

The shift in positioning was not incidental. By late 2023 and into 2024, the data centre infrastructure build-out driven by generative AI workloads had begun producing visible, documented pressure on utility interconnection queues across major US markets. Hyperscale operators and the project developers serving them faced multi-year waits for grid interconnect capacity at a moment when their power demand timelines were measured in months. On-site dispatchable generation — gas-fired units capable of bridging the gap between construction completion and permanent grid connection — was emerging as an active procurement category.

Capstone Energy+'s microturbine product line was, by this point, a 35-year-old technology with a documented field record across oil and gas, industrial cogeneration, and district energy. Its post-emergence strategic communications began positioning that record explicitly against the data centre bridge-power opportunity.

---

What the long arc of Capstone's corporate history produced, as of the December 2023 emergence, was this: a mature, field-proven distributed power technology developed across more than three decades; a public-company tenure characterised by genuine commercial adoption in multiple end markets but unbroken operating losses that accumulated past $1 billion; two corporate renames reflecting successive strategic pivots — from turbine hardware manufacturer to green-energy service integrator to dispatchable-power infrastructure provider; and a restructured equity now held by former creditors, trading on OTCQX rather than NASDAQ, at a company a fraction of the size its NASDAQ-era overhead implied. The company that filed in Delaware in September 2023 was not a failed technology. It was a proven technology that had never resolved the commercial tension between niche-market demand and the cost structure of a listed industrial enterprise. Whether Capstone Energy+ can resolve that tension under its post-emergence structure, in a market newly animated by AI data centre power demand, is the central question this dossier addresses.

chapters.title: Microturbine product lines, EaaS contracting, and customer applications
chapters.body:
## The microturbine product architecture

Capstone's product catalogue, largely unchanged in its structural logic since the company commercialised its first unit in the late 1990s, spans six nameplate configurations ranging from 30 kilowatts to 1.2 megawatts. Each unit shares a common mechanical premise: a single-shaft, high-speed turbine rotating on air bearings — compressed air cushions that replace the oil-lubricated ball and sleeve bearings found in conventional rotating machinery. The consequence of that design choice, which the company has long treated as its primary competitive differentiator against reciprocating engine alternatives, is a drivetrain with no liquid lubrication system, dramatically reduced scheduled maintenance intervals, and fewer mechanical failure modes during continuous operation.

The entry-level C30 delivers 30 kilowatts and was, for much of the company's early history, the unit through which Capstone established its reference base in niche applications — remote power, oil-field instrumentation, early CHP trials. The C65 (65 kW) occupied a similar niche applications tier. Both units were rendered commercially marginal in later years as the economics of scale pushed customers toward larger configurations; the C30 and C65 appear largely as legacy product in post-emergence communications, though they remain catalogued.

The practical workhorse of the fleet is the C200S, a 200-kilowatt unit whose modular footprint made it the basis for Capstone's packaged multi-turbine systems. The Signature Series — designated C600S, C800S, and C1000S — are factory-integrated packages combining three, four, or five C200S modules within a common enclosure with shared power electronics, control architecture, and heat recovery hardware. The C1000S delivers one megawatt from a configuration roughly twenty feet in length, a factor that matters materially at constrained urban and industrial sites. The C1200S, rated at 1.2 megawatts, represents the top of the single-enclosure product line and was introduced to compete more directly with small gas turbines and large reciprocating generator sets in the 750 kW–1.5 MW range. Packaged microgrid systems combining multiple C1000S or C1200S units with inverter hardware, battery storage, and supervisory control software extend the addressable capacity to several megawatts at a single site.

## Technology characteristics and competitive positioning

The air-bearing architecture eliminates oil changes and oil-related consumable costs, and Capstone has historically cited maintenance intervals measured in hours-between-overhaul that compare favourably against natural gas reciprocating engines of equivalent output. That advantage is most pronounced in remote and difficult-to-service applications — upstream oil and gas sites, for instance — where the total cost of dispatching maintenance technicians over a multi-year operating contract can be substantial.

Combustion characteristics also distinguish the microturbine from reciprocating competitors. Capstone's units operate with lean-premix combustion at relatively low flame temperatures, yielding nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions that the company has consistently certified below nine parts per million, and in some configurations below five parts per million, without selective catalytic reduction aftertreatment. In air-quality-sensitive jurisdictions — California's South Coast Air Quality Management District being the canonical example — that profile opens market access that diesel gensets or older gas reciprocating engines cannot match without costly emissions control equipment.

Fuel flexibility is a third axis of differentiation. The turbine combustor tolerates a wide range of gaseous fuel compositions: pipeline natural gas, wellhead or associated gas (which can contain heavy hydrocarbons and vary in Btu content), biogas from anaerobic digestion, landfill gas, and, in tested configurations, hydrogen-enriched blends. The practical implication is that a single product line can address markedly different customer fuel economics — the upstream oil producer seeking to monetise gas that would otherwise be flared, the wastewater authority generating biogas from sewage treatment, and the industrial customer purchasing pipeline gas for cogeneration.

Electrical efficiency at full load on a C200S is approximately 33 percent, lower than large combined-cycle turbines but competitive for small-scale distributed applications where the alternative is a grid connection with associated transmission losses and demand charges. When waste heat from the turbine exhaust — typically exiting at 500–600 degrees Fahrenheit — is recovered through a heat recovery unit for process heat or absorption chilling, aggregate system efficiency can reach 70 to 80 percent, a figure that materially improves the economics against grid power-plus-boiler combinations in many CHP applications.

## The EaaS contracting model

Capstone's Energy-as-a-Service offering, developed progressively during the final years before the Chapter 11 filing and carried forward as a stated priority under the post-emergence management structure, restructures the traditional capital-sale transaction into a long-term service contract. Under the EaaS model, Capstone or an authorised distributor installs, owns, and operates the microturbine system at a customer's facility. The customer pays for delivered energy — kilowatt-hours of electricity and, where applicable, thermal output — under a multi-year agreement, typically structured over seven to fifteen years, rather than purchasing the equipment outright.

The strategic logic for Capstone is straightforward: EaaS converts a lumpy, project-dependent equipment revenue stream into contracted recurring service revenue, smoothing cash flow and, in principle, supporting a more predictable financial profile. For customers — particularly in the industrial and commercial segments where capital allocation committees scrutinise balance sheet additions — the model reduces the up-front barrier to adoption and transfers technology and maintenance risk back to the vendor.

Segment-level disclosure of EaaS contract value, backlog, or revenue contribution as a distinct line item has been limited in Capstone's OTCQX filings through the period covered by this dossier. The company has disclosed EaaS as a strategic priority and cited customer wins in IR communications, but the absence of the detailed segment reporting required of NASDAQ- or NYSE-listed companies means that external assessment of the EaaS revenue conversion trajectory is constrained by the disclosure environment. Investors relying solely on public filings encounter a material information gap on this dimension.

## Oil and gas: the core installed base

The oil and gas vertical has historically represented Capstone's largest and most durable customer segment. The core application is associated gas utilisation at upstream well sites: natural gas produced co-mingled with crude oil that, in the absence of pipeline takeaway infrastructure or economic incentive to process, operators would otherwise flare or vent. Installing a Capstone microturbine at a well pad converts that gas stream into on-site electricity — powering pumps, compression, instrumentation, and worker accommodation — without requiring a utility grid connection. The economics are governed by the spread between the cost of flaring (regulatory, reputational, and operational) and the value of the electricity displaced; in active shale basins with active flaring-reduction regulation, that spread has supported robust demand for the product.

Midstream applications extend the footprint: compression stations, gas processing facilities, and pipeline measurement stations have deployed Capstone units where the combination of fuel availability, remote location, and emissions compliance requirements makes reciprocating alternatives less attractive. Drilling rig power, where the rig itself generates electricity for its own operations from wellhead gas, represents a more episodic but recurring application.

The oil and gas segment is also where Capstone's fuel flexibility is most commercially valuable. Associated gas composition varies widely by basin and by well; the turbine's tolerance for fuel variability reduces the conditioning requirement and lowers the total installed cost relative to reciprocating competitors that require tighter fuel specifications.

## Industrial cogeneration, district energy, and hospitality

Industrial CHP has been the second major customer category throughout Capstone's commercial history. The application is straightforward: a C200S or Signature Series unit provides base-load or near-base-load power generation at a manufacturing or processing facility, while exhaust heat is recovered for steam, hot water, or direct process heating. Food and beverage processing, pharmaceuticals, and light manufacturing have all appeared in the company's reference case library. The economics are most compelling where the facility operates continuously, has a stable thermal load, and faces high grid electricity tariffs with significant demand charge components.

University campuses, hospital complexes, and district energy schemes represent a related but distinct sub-segment. These customers typically require high-reliability baseload generation, often have both heating and cooling loads amenable to absorption chilling from exhaust heat, and operate under sustainability mandates that favour lower-emissions distributed generation. Hospitality — hotels and resorts with continuous hot water, heating, and power requirements — follows similar logic.

## The emerging AI data centre opportunity

The post-emergence strategic communications from Capstone Energy+ placed notable emphasis on AI data centre backup and bridge power as an incremental customer category. The thesis tracks a well-documented infrastructure constraint: hyperscale data centre operators pursuing gigawatt-scale capacity expansions in the 2023–2026 period encountered utility interconnect queues extending to three, four, or more years at preferred sites across the United States. Operators under competitive pressure to bring AI training and inference capacity online could not wait for grid connections. Dispatchable on-site generation — gas-fired, low-emissions, capable of meeting air quality permit requirements in constrained jurisdictions — represented one technical pathway.

Capstone's Signature Series and packaged multi-megawatt systems are positioned, in the company's framing, to serve this need: multi-MW configurations assembled from C1000S or C1200S modules, fuelled by pipeline natural gas, capable of operating in island mode without grid synchronisation, and meeting air quality thresholds that would disqualify diesel backup generator arrays in markets like California. The low-maintenance air-bearing architecture reduces operating burden during potentially multi-year pre-interconnect operating periods.

What the public record through the May 2026 snapshot date does not fully establish is the extent to which this positioning translated into signed contracts, awarded projects, or recognised revenue from the hyperscale or co-location data centre segment. OTCQX disclosure discipline does not require the customer-level or segment-level transparency that would allow external investors to size the contribution. The AI data centre narrative is coherent and structurally plausible; its financial materialisation, as of the frozen window, remains incompletely evidenced in Capstone Energy+'s public filings.

chapters.title: Pre-Chapter-11 trajectory, post-emergence cap table, and the EaaS conversion path
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Band That Never Translated Into Cash

For most of Capstone Turbine's two-decade run as a public company, the financial narrative followed a pattern sophisticated investors in small-cap industrial technology would recognise immediately: credible product, real customers, recurring revenue that never converted to operating profitability. The four fiscal years immediately preceding the September 2023 Chapter 11 filing traced a revenue band between roughly $73 million and $95 million — wide enough to suggest a functioning business, narrow enough to signal that scale was not happening.

Fiscal year 2022 (ending March 2022) represented the high-water mark of that period at approximately $95 million in revenue, a figure Capstone attributed in part to energy market tailwinds and demand recovery from the pandemic disruption that had compressed the FY2021 result to approximately $73 million. Fiscal year 2020 had closed at approximately $75 million. By fiscal year 2023 — ending March 2023, the final full-year period before the bankruptcy filing — revenue had retreated to approximately $77 million, unwinding most of the FY2022 gain.

| Fiscal Year (ending March) | Revenue (USD millions) |
|---|---|
| FY2020 | ~$75 |
| FY2021 | ~$73 |
| FY2022 | ~$95 |
| FY2023 | ~$77 |

*Source: Financials prep data derived from Capstone Green Energy disclosures; figures approximate pending individual 10-K reconciliation.*

What those revenue numbers did not show was a path to cash generation. Capstone had carried operating losses throughout its public-company tenure stretching back to its 2000 listing — a structural feature of microturbine economics that the company's own disclosures repeatedly flagged as a going-concern risk. The underlying technology was not experimental; the C65, C200S, and C1000S product families had logged cumulative installed-hours across oil and gas, cogeneration, and district energy applications over years. The problem was not technical immaturity. It was that the capital structure of an equipment manufacturer selling into project-finance-sensitive energy markets left persistent working capital tension between order intake, production expenditure, and customer-payment cycles.

**Note on operating loss magnitude:** Specific quarterly and annual operating loss figures for each fiscal year through FY2023 are derivable from Capstone Green Energy's NASDAQ-era 10-K and 10-Q filings via SEC EDGAR; those filings constitute the primary source for precise loss quantum and gross margin trajectory. The prep data for this dossier does not reproduce those line items, and the dossier declines to estimate them.

## What Broke in 2023

The September 28, 2023 Chapter 11 filing in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware was the formal acknowledgment of a liquidity crisis that had been building through a combination of pressures. Capstone's post-filing disclosures and the bankruptcy court record identified several converging factors: tightened liquidity, customer receivable concerns, and broader operational scaling challenges. The oil and gas segment — a meaningful portion of Capstone's project base, particularly associated-gas utilisation at upstream well sites — had historically involved project customers whose own cash cycles were sensitive to commodity price movement. When receivable collection slowed, a company with Capstone's operating loss structure had limited buffer to absorb the lag.

The filing was structured as a prepackaged Chapter 11, a mechanism that front-loads creditor negotiation before the formal court process and correspondingly compresses the in-court timeline. Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group had emerged as the principal pre-filing creditor, and the prepackaged plan reflected an agreement between Capstone and its senior lending group that had been substantially negotiated before the September filing date. The practical consequence was speed: Capstone emerged from Chapter 11 on December 7, 2023 — a roughly ten-week in-court period that is compact even by prepackaged standards.

Prepackaged structures of this type carry a predictable distributional outcome for legacy equity holders. Pre-Chapter-11 common stockholders in a company with Capstone's balance sheet profile — persistent operating losses, senior secured debt that exceeded recoverable enterprise value at the time of filing — received substantially wiped-out treatment, consistent with standard absolute priority enforcement in prepackaged restructurings. The reorganised entity emerged with a new equity base comprising former creditors, led by Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group's converted position alongside other creditors whose claims were similarly restructured into reorganised equity.

**Disclosure gap:** The precise post-emergence ownership table — percentage holdings of Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending versus other creditor groups, any management equity incentive pool, any retained stub equity for legacy holders — has not been reproduced in detail in the OTCQX-cadence disclosures available as of the May 2026 snapshot date. The OTCQX market imposes materially lower public reporting obligations than the NASDAQ listing Capstone held pre-bankruptcy, and the company's post-emergence filings reflect that reduced cadence. Investors requiring a precise cap table should engage directly with Capstone Energy+ investor relations.

## The OTCQX Entity: What Post-Emergence Disclosure Confirms and What It Does Not

The surviving entity, listed on OTCQX under the ticker CGEH following the December 2023 emergence and subsequently rebranded as Capstone Energy+ Inc, represents a structurally lighter disclosure regime than sophisticated investors accustomed to NASDAQ-listed industrials will be familiar with. OTCQX requires audited annual financials and periodic disclosures but does not impose the quarterly 10-Q cadence or the 8-K current-reporting obligations of an SEC reporting company. The result is a material information gap relative to the pre-bankruptcy disclosure record.

Post-emergence revenue trajectory and cash position as of the May 2026 snapshot are areas where this dossier explicitly defers to direct verification via current Capstone Energy+ IR communications and any OTCQX-filed annual report for the fiscal period ending March 2025 or March 2026. The prep data confirms the company's post-emergence strategic refocus and the AI data centre positioning but does not reproduce audited post-emergence financials. Any investor model built on assumptions about post-emergence revenue or balance sheet cash should treat those figures as requiring primary verification.

## The EaaS Conversion: Economics and Strategic Rationale

The 2021 rename from Capstone Turbine Corporation to Capstone Green Energy had signalled a strategic intent to move from equipment-sale economics toward Energy-as-a-Service contracting, and the post-emergence Capstone Energy+ identity continued that trajectory. The distinction matters financially and the EaaS model's appeal to a post-restructuring equity base is straightforward to articulate even where the precise revenue mix remains undisclosed.

An equipment-sale transaction — Capstone ships microturbines, customer pays for hardware and installation, relationship continues through a service contract — concentrates revenue recognition at point of sale and exposes the manufacturer to working capital intensity around production, shipping, and customer payment cycles. The FY2022-to-FY2023 revenue compression from approximately $95 million to $77 million illustrates the volatility inherent in project-sale timing.

An EaaS contract reframes the economics: Capstone or a Capstone-affiliated financing vehicle retains ownership of the generation asset, deploys it at the customer site, and charges for energy delivered or capacity made available over a multi-year contract term, typically ranging from five to fifteen years depending on project type and customer creditworthiness. The customer converts a capital expenditure into an operating expenditure. Capstone converts a lump-sum equipment sale into a recurring revenue stream.

The credit implications of this transition are non-trivial. EaaS projects require upfront capital to procure and install generation assets before recurring revenue begins accruing. For a post-restructuring entity with a reorganised balance sheet and constrained access to capital markets, the pace at which EaaS deployment can be funded — whether through the company's own balance sheet, project finance structures, or third-party energy financing partners — directly governs how quickly the recurring revenue base can grow. Capstone Energy+'s ability to originate EaaS projects at scale will be a function of its post-emergence financial capacity as much as its commercial origination capability, and the current disclosure record does not permit a precise assessment of either constraint.

**Disclosure gap:** The current EaaS versus equipment-sale revenue mix, backlog composition, and contracted EaaS megawatts or project count as of the May 2026 snapshot are not detailed in the available prep data. Investors should query Capstone Energy+ IR directly for current pipeline and backlog disclosure.

## The Structural Inheritance

What Capstone Energy+ carried out of bankruptcy was a technology platform with a multi-decade commercial track record — microturbines operating in oil fields, hospitals, university campuses, and cogeneration applications across multiple continents — a restructured balance sheet that eliminated the senior debt burden that had contributed to the liquidity crisis, and a reorganised equity base whose return expectations were priced to the post-emergence entry point rather than the pre-bankruptcy capital structure. That combination is the starting point from which any assessment of the EaaS conversion path and the AI data centre opportunity must be constructed.

The persistent challenge is that Capstone has been, for its entire public-company life, a business that required more capital than its operating cash flows generated. The question the post-emergence equity base must answer is whether the EaaS revenue model, applied to an AI data centre market that did not exist as a meaningful revenue category during Capstone's NASDAQ years, changes that equation — or whether the structural inheritance is more durable than the rebranding suggests.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
The central analytical challenge in valuing Capstone Energy+ is not a shortage of frameworks but a shortage of data. As an OTCQX-listed post-Chapter-11 entity, CGEH operates under materially reduced public disclosure obligations relative to its former NASDAQ-listed incarnation — and relative to every named peer in the distributed power generation sector. Standard valuation inputs that analysts take for granted on exchange-listed companies — audited annual reports filed on tight schedules, quarterly earnings calls with management guidance, consensus sell-side estimates — are either absent, delayed, or available only in summary form through the OTCQX disclosure portal. Any multiples derived from publicly available CGEH data carry this asterisk, and sophisticated investors should treat them accordingly.

## Market Capitalisation and the Float Problem

Establishing even a baseline market capitalisation for CGEH requires working around two compounding uncertainties: the post-emergence share structure and the thinness of OTCQX trading volumes. Under the prepackaged Chapter 11 plan confirmed in December 2023, pre-petition common equity was substantially extinguished and reorganised equity was issued to former creditors, with Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group as the principal pre-filing secured creditor. The precise post-emergence share count, par value, and any warrants or management incentive equity attached to the plan of reorganisation were disclosed in the bankruptcy court docket in the District of Delaware — but those filings are not routinely synthesised into Bloomberg terminal data or EDGAR summaries accessible to most equity-market participants. This is a material disclosure gap with no easy workaround.

What can be reasonably inferred: post-Chapter-11 entities that emerge via prepackaged restructuring with a single dominant creditor-turned-equity-holder typically carry a thin public float, with the majority of reorganised equity concentrated among a small number of former creditors who have no particular incentive to sell into thin OTC markets. Price discovery on CGEH is therefore episodic rather than continuous, and any spot market capitalisation figure derived from the OTCQX last-trade price may reflect a thin cross rather than a market-clearing value.

Working from the revenue trajectory documented in the financial history chapter, a rough triangulation is nonetheless possible. If one applies a sector-floor revenue multiple of 0.3x–0.5x trailing revenue to the approximate post-emergence revenue run rate — itself uncertain, but likely in the $60M–$80M range given the operational disruption of the Chapter 11 process and the subsequent strategic refocus — the implied enterprise value falls in the $20M–$40M range. Back out net debt, which was substantially restructured in the emergence, and the market capitalisation range is correspondingly narrow. This is a revenue-multiple floor, not a thesis price. It reflects the market assigning minimal credit for growth or margin expansion. Readers with OTCQX terminal access should verify the last reported share count against any available IR disclosure; no precision figure can be stated with confidence as of 23 May 2026.

## Historical Multiple Context and the Re-Rating Question

The pre-Chapter-11 Capstone entity — trading as CPST on NASDAQ through 2021, then as CGRN on NASDAQ until the September 2023 filing — carried a consistent multiple profile reflecting persistent operating losses. Across the FY2020–FY2023 period, with revenue ranging from $73M to $95M, the company never achieved GAAP operating profitability at scale. EV/Revenue multiples for CPST/CGRN hovered broadly in the 0.4x–1.2x range depending on market sentiment toward clean-energy and distributed-power themes. The company received a brief sentiment re-rating during the 2021 clean-energy rally, touching the higher end of that range as the Capstone Green Energy rebrand coincided with peak ESG enthusiasm, before a progressive de-rating as operating losses persisted and the macro rate environment turned.

The post-emergence entity, CGEH, does not inherit a directly comparable multiple history — it is effectively a new equity with a new capital structure. But the underlying business characteristics — microturbine OEM plus EaaS integrator, predominantly North American commercial and industrial exposure, with an emerging AI data centre vertical — are continuous with the prior entity. The historical range provides a ceiling for what a market-sceptical scenario assigns; the AI data centre thesis and EaaS recurring revenue conversion are the arguments for trading above that ceiling.

## Peer-Group Comparison

The table below compares CGEH against five named peers across the distributed stationary power and backup generation space. Multiples reflect approximate conditions as of May 2026 based on public filings and market data, with significant rounding given CGEH's disclosure limitations. CGEH figures are explicitly flagged as estimates.

| Company | Ticker | Approx. Market Cap | EV/Revenue (TTM) | EV/EBITDA | Business mix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Capstone Energy+ | CGEH (OTCQX) | ~$25M–$50M est. | ~0.4x–0.7x est. | N/M (losses) | Microturbine OEM + EaaS microgrid + AI data centre bridge |
| Bloom Energy | BE (NYSE) | ~$3.5B–$4.5B | ~3.5x–4.5x | ~25x–35x | Fuel cell distributed power, EaaS, data centre penetration |
| FuelCell Energy | FCEL (NASDAQ) | ~$200M–$400M | ~3x–5x | N/M (losses) | Fuel cell stationary power, utility-scale, EaaS |
| Tecogen | TGEN (NASDAQ) | ~$80M–$120M | ~1.0x–1.5x | ~12x–18x | CHP microgrid systems, industrial and commercial |
| Generac Holdings | GNRC (NYSE) | ~$8B–$10B | ~2.0x–2.5x | ~14x–18x | Backup power generation, residential and C&I |
| Cummins | CMI (NYSE) | ~$35B–$45B | ~1.5x–2.0x | ~10x–14x | Diversified power equipment, generators, engines |

The most analytically useful comparison is with Tecogen — a broadly comparable business model, serving commercial and industrial customers with CHP microgrid systems — which trades at 1.0x–1.5x EV/Revenue with evidence of EBITDA profitability. The gap between CGEH's implied 0.4x–0.7x and Tecogen's 1.0x–1.5x represents, in rough terms, the restructuring discount and disclosure penalty. If Capstone Energy+ can demonstrate operational stabilisation, EaaS contract accumulation, and a credible path to EBITDA breakeven, a re-rating toward Tecogen-equivalent multiples represents the near-term valuation recovery story.

Bloom Energy is the aspirational comparable — a company that successfully executed the EaaS pivot for distributed stationary power and attracted hyperscaler data centre contracts at scale. Bloom trades at a substantial premium on both EV/Revenue and EV/EBITDA, but the comparison is instructive: it illustrates what a successful EaaS distributed power operator with demonstrated data centre penetration can ultimately command in a public market. That multiple is not a near-term target for CGEH; it is the upper bound of what the thesis ultimately reaches for.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Current Price Implies

A simplified DCF framing is useful less for precision than for identifying the embedded assumptions. Working from a base-case revenue estimate of approximately $70M–$80M for the fiscal year ending March 2026, applying a conservative 5%–8% long-run revenue growth rate reflecting gradual EaaS contract ramp plus modest AI data centre contribution, a discount rate of 13%–15% appropriate for a small-cap post-restructuring entity with limited public disclosure, and a terminal EV/EBITDA exit multiple in the 10x–12x range — the implied equity value at current market capitalisation levels suggests the market is pricing in either persistent operating losses for multiple years, or a meaningful probability of further operational distress.

The current market-implied scenario is approximately: no meaningful margin expansion for three to four years, followed by modest profitability at a scale broadly similar to today. That is the embedded bear case the current price reflects. It assigns near-zero probability to the AI data centre bridge power opportunity delivering at scale, and minimal credit for EaaS recurring revenue growth compounding forward.

## Bull / Base / Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $80M–$120M implied enterprise value.** Revenue reaches $100M–$110M by FY2027 (ending March 2027), driven by two or three anchor AI data centre bridge-power contracts and continued EaaS backlog conversion. EBITDA turns positive at $8M–$12M. The market re-rates to 1.2x–1.5x EV/Revenue, consistent with Tecogen or a modest premium given the AI data centre narrative. This scenario requires hyperscaler or co-location contract execution within 12–18 months and no further capital structure complications. The key assumption is that the utility interconnect queue problem at major data centre markets — Northern Virginia, Phoenix, Dallas, and the Southeast — persists long enough that Capstone's on-site dispatchable microturbine solution becomes genuinely cost-competitive with alternatives. Applied multiple: ~1.2x–1.5x forward revenue.

**Base case — $30M–$55M implied enterprise value.** Revenue stabilises at $75M–$85M over the next two years as EaaS conversions proceed at a measured pace and AI data centre interest advances to pilot-stage discussions but not yet to full contract. EBITDA remains near breakeven or marginally negative. The multiple stays in the 0.5x–0.8x EV/Revenue range as the market waits for proof-of-concept data centre delivery. This is the "show me" scenario — the thesis is intact but unproven, and the stock drifts sideways with high volatility around any contract announcement. Applied multiple: ~0.5x–0.8x forward revenue.

**Bear case — $10M–$25M implied enterprise value, or further distress.** Revenue contracts below $70M as Chapter 11 disruption proves more durable than expected, key customer relationships erode, and the AI data centre opportunity is captured by better-capitalised alternatives — Bloom Energy fuel cells, Cummins generator sets, or Caterpillar-packaged solutions — that can offer lower per-kWh economics or superior warranty programmes. EBITDA remains negative. The multiple compresses toward 0.2x–0.4x EV/Revenue as restructuring optionality erodes; the post-emergence creditor-holders explore secondary exits into thin OTC liquidity; and the company revisits its capital structure within 24 months. Applied multiple: ~0.2x–0.4x forward revenue, with non-trivial probability weight on a second restructuring event.

## What the Market is Currently Pricing In

The current CGEH implied valuation — whatever figure OTC trading produces at any given moment — reflects a market that has simultaneously assigned a material discount for the Chapter 11 stigma and reduced disclosure cadence, assigned near-zero value to the AI data centre thesis absent demonstrated contract wins, and acknowledged the EaaS recurring revenue model as directionally positive but unproven at the scale required to move the multiple. The gap between the dossier's read and apparent market consensus is concentrated in that AI data centre optionality: if even one or two anchor hyperscaler or co-location operator contracts convert — with the public announcement and economic disclosure that would follow — the disclosure deficit narrows sharply, sell-side attention becomes possible, and the re-rating catalyst arrives. Until then, CGEH trades precisely as it should: as a post-restructuring distributed power operator with a speculative upside story, priced accordingly, and requiring patience or a near-term catalyst to resolve the discount.

chapters.title: Pre-Chapter-11 quarters through emergence and post-emergence trajectory
chapters.body:
## A Long Ascent Interrupted: Revenues, Restructuring, and Rebirth

Capstone Green Energy entered its fiscal year 2022 — the twelve months ended March 31, 2022 — as something that had eluded the Van Nuys, California microturbine maker for most of its publicly traded life: a company approaching genuine commercial scale. Revenue for the period reached approximately $95 million, a high-water mark across the company's post-2000 NASDAQ tenure, and the Energy-as-a-Service rental fleet that management had staked the company's future on was expanding rapidly. The company reported 9-month fiscal-2023 revenues of $59.0 million through December 2022, up 9.5 percent year-over-year, and the rental fleet under contract had grown 126 percent year-over-year to 40 megawatts. Then, almost without warning, the wheels came off.

## The Quarters Before the Fall

Quarterly results in fiscal year 2023 told a story of operational fragility behind the revenue headline. First-quarter revenue of $18.7 million was 16 percent above the year-ago period; the second quarter at $20.8 million added a further 21 percent gain. But the third quarter, covering October through December 2022, slipped to $19.6 million, down five percent year-on-year, as supply-chain disruptions, elevated freight costs, and component shortages compressed product shipments. Gross margin for that nine-month stretch clocked 16 percent — well below the 25-percent target management had consistently described to investors.

Darren Jamison, who had served as president and chief executive since 2006 — a 16-year tenure that spanned the original Capstone Turbine identity, the 2021 rebranding to Capstone Green Energy, and the entire EaaS pivot — acknowledged the pressure directly. "Although product shipments during the third quarter were challenged as we continue to battle supply chain disruptions and higher costs," Jamison said in the Q3 fiscal-2023 earnings release, "I expect this will begin to be offset by our price increases implemented at the end of January." He described EaaS as "a pivotal factor in achieving this goal." The full-year fiscal-2023 result came in at approximately $77 million — a drop of roughly $18 million from the fiscal-2022 peak.

Those headwinds also masked a deteriorating balance sheet. Pre-petition debt and accrued interest stood at $56.0 million, principally owed under an amended and restated note purchase agreement dated October 1, 2020, with Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group, L.P. as collateral agent and its affiliate Broad Street Credit Holdings LLC as the lending counterparty. Liquidity cushions were thin.

| Fiscal Year (ended March 31) | Revenue | Gross Margin | Adj. EBITDA | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | ~$75M | n/d | n/d | Pre-rebrand |
| FY2021 | ~$73M | n/d | n/d | COVID disruption |
| FY2022 | ~$95M | n/d | n/d | Revenue peak |
| FY2023 | ~$77M | ~16%* | n/d | Supply-chain drag |
| FY2024 | $91.2M | 16% | ($0.5M) | Straddles Ch.11; incl. $32.5M reorg. gain |
| FY2025 | $85.6M | 27% | $7.9M | First positive full-year EBITDA |

*Nine-month figure through December 2022. Full-year margin not separately disclosed pre-filing. Sources: [Capstone Green Energy Q3 FY2023 press release](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/3994/); [Capstone Green Energy FY2025 annual results](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/4040/).

## The Jamison Departure and the Filing

The first public signal of the coming restructuring came on August 14, 2023, when Capstone announced that Jamison had resigned from both the chief executive role and the board, effective August 22, with no successor named from inside the organisation. Robert C. Flexon — a veteran utility-sector executive and former chief executive of Dynegy and Foster & Wheeler, who also served as chair of PG&E Corp. and as a director of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas — had been appointed executive chairman days earlier and now assumed the additional title of interim president and CEO. Lead independent director Denise Wilson offered a terse send-off: "The board thanks Darren for his 16 years of service at Capstone." The company disclosed no reason for the departure.

Thirty-six days later, on September 28, 2023, Capstone Green Energy Corporation and its wholly-owned subsidiaries filed voluntary petitions for relief under Chapter 11 of the United States Bankruptcy Code in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. The filing was accompanied by a Transaction Support Agreement executed the same day with Broad Street Credit Holdings LLC and Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group in their respective capacities as consenting lender and collateral agent. Capstone simultaneously disclosed $3.0 million of new-money bridge financing provided one week earlier, on September 22, with a committed $12.0 million debtor-in-possession facility available upon court approval — total DIP support of $15.0 million.

The restructuring mechanics were pre-negotiated and narrow. Pre-petition debt of $56.0 million was to be reduced to $25.0 million, a haircut of $31.0 million. The plan split the enterprise in two: the legacy Capstone Green Energy Corporation would be renamed Capstone Distributor Support Services Corporation and taken private; its subsidiary, Capstone Turbine International, Inc., would be renamed Capstone Green Energy Holdings, Inc. and serve as the continuing publicly-listed entity for SEC reporting purposes. Existing NASDAQ common stockholders were to receive one share of the new public company per share cancelled — preserving equity participation at roughly 62.5 percent of the reorganised operating entity, with the consenting lender taking the remaining 37.5 percent stake. That structure was materially more equity-preserving than the zero-recovery outcome common in contested Chapter 11 proceedings.

Flexon framed the filing in characteristically terse language:

> "The transactions contemplated by the TSA have been carefully designed to preserve and enhance value for all stakeholders."

## Emergence: 70 Days

Court approval of the prepackaged plan came in late November 2023, and Capstone emerged from Chapter 11 on December 7, 2023 — approximately 70 days after the initial filing, faster than typical for operational restructurings of comparable scale. At emergence the company secured an additional $7.0 million in new-money financing on top of the exit facility, which comprised $12.0 million in new debt plus $8.0 million of pre-petition debt converted to exit notes, against a $5.0 million revolving credit facility. Total post-emergence funded debt stood at $25.0 million.

CFO John Juric, who carried through the restructuring into the new entity, acknowledged the disruption to customers and vendors directly:

> "I would like to express my appreciation to our customers, vendors, and business partners for their patience."

Capstone Green Energy Corporation's NASDAQ listing was terminated; shares migrated first to the OTC Expert Market and then, beginning January 2, 2025, to the OTC Pink Open Market under the ticker CGEH. The step up to the OTCQX Best Market — which would restore institutional accessibility at a higher reporting standard — remained a stated objective through the close of the frozen-snapshot window in May 2026, with management noting in the fiscal-2025 annual release that it was "working to elevate the positioning of the Company's stock to the OTC:QX market."

## Reporting Gaps and the FY2024 Transition Year

The move to OTCQX reporting cadence imposed a materially reduced disclosure rhythm relative to the NASDAQ-listed predecessor. The fiscal-2024 10-K, covering the twelve months ended March 31, 2024 — a period that straddled the Chapter 11 filing, the DIP process, and the emergence — was filed late, in autumn 2024. CFO Juric described it as "a pivotal milestone in our path toward full compliance with SEC reporting requirements." No revenue or operating-metric figures appeared in the accompanying press release; investors had to navigate the underlying 10-K directly for financial detail. Full-year fiscal-2024 revenue, which emerged in the fiscal-2025 comparatives, stood at $91.2 million, a figure that blended the final pre-filing quarters with the post-emergence operating period and was inflated by a $32.5 million reorganisation gain that generated $7.4 million of statutory net income against an underlying adjusted EBITDA of negative $0.5 million.

## The Canino Chapter and the First Positive EBITDA

Robert Flexon handed off day-to-day management on March 11, 2024, when Vince Canino joined as president and CEO. Canino brought more than thirty years of energy-sector experience — most recently as chief operating officer of ESS Tech, Inc., a long-duration iron-flow battery developer — and transitioned closely with Flexon before the latter moved to non-executive chairman on April 1, 2024.

The fiscal-2025 results, released in 2025, delivered the milestone that had defined a generation of Capstone management aspirations. Full-year revenue of $85.6 million fell modestly from the prior year's $91.2 million, but gross margin expanded to 27 percent from 16 percent, operating cash flow turned positive at $7.7 million, and adjusted EBITDA reached $7.9 million. Canino did not understate the significance:

> "In all of its 37-year history, the Company has never delivered positive Adjusted EBITDA over a full fiscal year."

He added: "We have changed the culture and truly changed the landscape of what Capstone's true potential is."

On the balance sheet, cash on hand grew to $8.7 million from $2.1 million a year earlier — a swing that provided the first credible liquidity buffer of the post-emergence period. The previously disclosed SEC investigation, which had added regulatory uncertainty through 2024, was closed with no action taken.

## Positioning Toward the Data-Centre Opportunity

Against this improving operational base, management's strategic communications increasingly pointed toward AI data-centre backup and bridge power as an addressable growth vector, driven by tightening utility interconnect queues across major US markets. In October 2025, Capstone formalised that positioning by announcing, at Data Center World Asia, an 800-volt direct-current microturbine engineered in partnership with Microgrids 4 AI, Inc., designed to interface with NVIDIA's Kyber and Rubin Ultra rack platforms and capable of scaling from sub-20-megawatt edge deployments to gigawatt-class AI campuses.

Canino characterised the product's rationale in terms of the shifting power architecture of hyperscale computing:

> "Our 800 VDC microturbine is designed for this new reality, building clean, reliable, redundant and direct high-voltage DC power."

Whether that product line translates into a material revenue contribution within the frozen-snapshot horizon remained undisclosed; no contract volumes, project bookings, or revenue guidance specific to the data-centre channel had appeared in public filings or press releases through May 23, 2026. The initiative nonetheless represented the clearest articulation of the post-emergence growth thesis that management had offered investors since the December 2023 exit from Chapter 11.

---

**Disclosure note:** Capstone Energy+ (CGEH) reports on an OTCQX cadence with materially reduced frequency and depth relative to its former NASDAQ-listed status. Quarterly earnings releases are published without associated analyst calls; the SEC investigation disclosure and the late filing of the FY2024 10-K both underscore the reduced transparency of the post-emergence reporting environment. Investors should treat the FY2024 revenue figure — which straddles the restructuring — and the accompanying net income as structurally non-comparable to pre- or post-filing periods.

chapters.title: Post-emergence executive team and the restructured-equity board
chapters.body:
## A Sixteen-Year Tenure Ends in Crisis

For the better part of two decades, Darren Jamison defined the Capstone Turbine identity. Appointed chief executive in 2007, Jamison presided over the company's expansion from a niche aerospace-derived turbine manufacturer into a global distributed-power platform — navigating the Capstone Green Energy rebrand in 2021 and building a distribution network spanning eighty-eight countries. By the time the company's financial position had deteriorated to the point of prepackaged bankruptcy, Jamison had logged roughly sixteen years in the chief executive role, an unusually long tenure for a small-cap industrials company. On August 14, 2023, Capstone Green Energy [announced his departure](https://www.capstonegreenenergy.com/news/press-releases/detail/4012/), effective August 22 — five weeks before the Chapter 11 filing in the District of Delaware. The board offered no strategic rationale for the separation beyond a standard statement of thanks for his years of service. [Turbomachinery Magazine](https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/ceo-resignation-leaves-vacancy-at-capstone-green-energy) noted at the time that the resignation left a leadership vacancy at a precarious moment.

## Flexon as Stabilising Force

Into the vacuum stepped Robert C. Flexon. A director since 2017 and board chair since 2021, Flexon was a credible operator: he had run Dynegy Inc. through its own bankruptcy restructuring and subsequent $3.3 billion sale to Vistra Energy, establishing a reputation as a utility-sector turnaround executive. On August 9, 2023, the board elevated him to Executive Chairman and, from the effective date of Jamison's resignation, to Interim President and Chief Executive Officer — a dual mandate that made him the company's de facto leader through the Chapter 11 process.

Flexon guided Capstone through the prepackaged reorganisation without meaningful operational disruption. The company emerged from Chapter 11 on December 7, 2023, with a restructured balance sheet, $7 million in fresh exit financing, and a new equity ownership structure in which former senior lender Goldman Sachs — whose credit facility had been converted into preferred equity in a newly formed subsidiary, Capstone Green Energy LLC — held a 62.5% controlling economic interest in the operating business. Predecessor common shareholders received one new share for each share cancelled, preserving a residual public equity stub that would eventually trade on the OTCQX under the ticker CGEH.

The emergence press release quoted Flexon: 

> "With Chapter 11 behind us and a much stronger financial position, we can now fully focus on our distribution partners."

The five-person board assembled at emergence reflected the new ownership realities. Alongside Flexon as Chairman, the [December 2023 announcement](https://www.capstoneenergyplus.com/news/press-releases/detail/4019/) named Denise M. Wilson as Lead Independent Director, and three additional directors: Yon Yoon Jorden, technology entrepreneur Ping Fu, and Robert F. Powelson. Wilson brought utility-sector operating credibility — she had served as Executive Vice President and President of Alternative Energy Businesses at NRG Energy from 2011 to 2016. Ping Fu, co-founder and former chief executive of 3D imaging software company Geomagic (acquired by 3D Systems in 2013), provided technology and entrepreneurship experience and also held a seat on the Live Nation Entertainment board. Powelson arrived with a distinctive regulatory pedigree: a former Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission chairman who served as a Federal Energy Regulatory Commissioner from 2017 to 2018, he had subsequently become President and Chief Executive of the National Association of Water Companies. His presence gave the post-emergence board a credible regulatory interface for an energy company navigating utility interconnect and distributed-generation permitting environments.

**Board composition at December 2023 emergence**

| Director | Role | Prior Relevant Background |
|---|---|---|
| Robert C. Flexon | Chairman & Interim CEO | Dynegy CEO; utility restructuring |
| Denise M. Wilson | Lead Independent Director | NRG Energy EVP; alternative energy |
| Yon Yoon Jorden | Director | Serial CFO; AdvancePCS, WellPoint |
| Ping Fu | Director | Geomagic founder/CEO; 3D Systems CSO |
| Robert F. Powelson | Director | FERC Commissioner; PA PUC Chairman |

Notably absent from the emergence board was any named representative of Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group or its affiliated entities, despite Goldman's preferred equity stake representing the dominant economic interest in the operating subsidiary. The Goldman position was structured at the subsidiary level rather than as direct common equity in the listed holding company; the OTCQX-listed CGEH held a minority residual claim on the economics until the restructuring was completed. This structural layering meant the Goldman economic interest was reflected in the capital structure rather than directly in boardroom representation — a governance arrangement that would generate friction in subsequent periods.

## The Canino Appointment

The permanent chief executive search concluded on March 11, 2024. [Capstone announced](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240312283880/en/Capstone-Green-Energy-Announces-Vince-Canino-as-its-President-and-Chief-Executive-Officer) the appointment of Vincent J. Canino as President and Chief Executive Officer and a member of the board, with an annual base salary approved by the Compensation and Human Capital Committee of $550,000. Flexon simultaneously transitioned from Executive Chairman to Non-Executive Chairman, a role he assumed April 1, 2024.

Canino brought over three decades of industrial power and thermal systems experience. He had spent roughly eight years as President and Chief Executive of the Smardt Chiller Group, where he oversaw global expansion in high-efficiency centrifugal chillers — a technology segment with significant overlap with the energy efficiency positioning Capstone sought to emphasise in its EaaS commercialisation strategy. Immediately prior to Capstone, he had served as Chief Operating Officer of ESS Inc. (NYSE: GWH), a long-duration iron-air energy storage developer, from September 2022 to March 2024, giving him direct exposure to the emerging energy storage and microgrid financing landscape. Earlier in his career he held vice-president roles at Trane. He holds a B.Tech in Mechanical Engineering Technology from SUNY Binghamton and an M.S. in Engineering Mechanics from Pennsylvania State University.

Also in February 2024, the board added John P. Miller as an independent director. Miller brought more than forty years of executive management across manufacturing, distribution, and transportation, including a stint as Chief Executive Officer of Power Solutions International, Inc. from 2017 to 2021 and senior vice-president roles at Navistar International. His appointment added both audit-committee depth and industrial-manufacturing operational experience.

## CFO Evolution

John J. Juric had been in place as Chief Financial Officer since March 6, 2023 — appointed in the final months before the Chapter 11 filing and carrying the company through the restructuring process. Juric brought more than twenty-five years of finance and manufacturing experience, having previously served as CFO of USALCO, a water-treatment chemistry provider, and in divisional CFO roles at Fiberweb. He remained CFO through the emergence, through the Canino appointment, and through the subsequent operating rebuild — until, on November 1, 2025, he resigned without stated cause. The simultaneous announcement on November 5, 2025 of Juric's departure and the subsequent governance events drew immediate investor attention.

Miller, who had served on the board's Audit Committee as its chair, was appointed Interim Chief Financial Officer effective November 2, 2025, assuming dual board and executive roles. No permanent CFO had been named as of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, leaving the finance function under interim leadership during a period of significant capital activity.

## A Board Fracture and Reset

The CFO departure was not the lead item in the November 2025 announcement. On October 30, 2025, Robert Flexon had resigned from the board entirely — the first clean break with the company he had steered through bankruptcy. The cited reason was blunt: a [disagreement over the company's strategic direction](https://www.tradingview.com/news/tradingview:020240f4f5f31:0-capstone-green-energy-announces-board-and-cfo-changes/), with Flexon having expressed concern about any alternative that diluted common stockholders without addressing the company's debt profile. The subtext was the board's active evaluation of capital-raise structures that would use preferred equity or convertible instruments to retire the legacy Goldman Sachs position — precisely the transaction that would close four months later. Robert Powelson was appointed Interim Chairman of the Board effective October 31, 2025.

Two further independent directors had by then joined the board. Christopher J. Close was appointed effective June 16, 2025, bringing the board to seven members. Close, then 59, had more than thirty-five years of senior financial leadership — CFO tenures at Noramco and Preferred Sands, earlier career finance roles at Exelon, Constellation Energy, and Airgas, and PricewaterhouseCoopers audit experience at the start of his career. He was appointed to chair the Audit Committee. At the August 12, 2025 virtual annual meeting of stockholders, Robert F. Beard was elected as a Class I director, bringing the board to eight members. Beard had retired as Chief Operating Officer of UGI Corporation and Chief Executive Officer of UGI Utilities, where he had directed a $1.3 billion midstream acquisition and led multi-billion-dollar capital programmes; he subsequently served on the Black Hills Corporation board. His addition aligned with Capstone's push to deepen midstream and utility relationships.

After Flexon's October departure the board stood at seven, a figure that proved significant when Monarch Alternative Capital's [investment of $112.5 million closed on March 31, 2026](https://ir.capstoneenergyplus.com/press-releases/detail/4066). The transaction redeemed the Goldman Sachs preferred equity in Capstone Green Energy LLC in full ($85 million of the proceeds), making the operating subsidiary a wholly-owned asset of the listed holding company for the first time since emergence. Under the securities purchase agreement, Monarch obtained the right to appoint two independent directors to a board fixed at seven members — a governance concession that, as of the frozen snapshot date, had not produced publicly named appointments. The composition of any Monarch-designated seats remained undisclosed in Capstone Energy+ IR communications through May 23, 2026.

## Disclosure Gaps

Several governance questions remain inadequately documented in Capstone Energy+'s public disclosures as of the snapshot date. Yon Yoon Jorden, who joined the board at the December 2023 emergence, no longer appeared on the company's IR management-team page; the timing and circumstances of her departure from the board were not the subject of any press release or 8-K filing traceable through the company's investor relations archive, leaving a gap in the governance record. The identity of any Monarch-appointed directors — given Monarch's contractual right to two seats on the seven-member board — had not been disclosed. And the permanent CFO search, presumably underway since November 2025, had not produced a public announcement. For a listed company with ambitions of graduating to a national securities exchange within twelve months of the March 2026 capital raise, those disclosure gaps are material: institutional investors accustomed to NYSE or NASDAQ governance standards will expect a permanent CFO, a fully disclosed director roster, and explicit committee assignment disclosure for any new board members before the listing application is credibly advanced.
