chapters.title: Oil-and-gas, industrial CHP, district energy, AI data centres, and the microturbine supply chain
chapters.body:
## Oil and Gas: The Anchor Segment

Throughout most of Capstone Turbine Corporation's publicly traded history, the oil and gas vertical was the company's largest revenue contributor, accounting for roughly 40 to 60 percent of annual product revenues in the years immediately preceding the Chapter 11 filing, according to the company's annual reports filed with the SEC during its NYSE listing period. The application that drove that concentration was deceptively straightforward: microturbines convert associated gas — the methane-rich byproduct that emerges at the wellhead alongside crude oil — into on-site electricity, eliminating flaring, reducing emissions, and powering pumps, compressors, and communications equipment at remote well pads where grid interconnection is economically impractical or physically unavailable.

The C200S and the packaged C600S and C1000S configurations became the workhorses of this segment. A single C1000S can run continuously on low-pressure associated gas at roughly 28-percent electrical efficiency, and because Capstone's air-bearing architecture eliminates oil lubrication from the rotating assembly, the units tolerate the lean maintenance schedules common at unmanned upstream sites. Capstone's public filings identified the Permian Basin, the Eagle Ford, and broader Appalachian shale plays as geographies where the installed base was concentrated in North America. Internationally, the company had material exposure to Russian upstream operators through a distributor relationship; that channel was severely disrupted following the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent rounds of Western export controls, and Capstone Green Energy's annual reports for fiscal years 2022 and 2023 explicitly cited Russia-related revenue deterioration as a material headwind. Specific named upstream customers have not been disclosed in any OTCQX filing reviewed within the frozen window; this is a persistent disclosure gap that reflects both the OTCQX reporting framework and Capstone's historic practice of aggregating customer data by vertical rather than by name.

Post-emergence under Capstone Energy+, the company has continued to emphasise the oil and gas segment in IR communications as a source of recurring service revenue from the installed base, even as new unit shipments to the segment remain constrained by the company's post-restructuring manufacturing capacity and working capital position. The installed base represents a service annuity — long-term parts and maintenance agreements, renewal of Factory Protection Plan contracts — that is structurally more durable than new-unit revenue during a capital-constrained period.

## Industrial Cogeneration: The CHP Installed Base

Combined heat and power installations constitute the second major customer pillar. In a CHP configuration, a Capstone microturbine generates electricity while the high-temperature exhaust — leaving the turbine at roughly 260 degrees Celsius after passing through the recuperator — is routed to a heat recovery unit to produce hot water or low-pressure steam for space heating, process heat, or absorption cooling. System-level efficiencies in a well-designed CHP installation can reach 70 to 80 percent, a figure that anchors the economic case for customers facing high grid electricity tariffs.

Capstone's industrial CHP customer base has historically encompassed food and beverage processing, pharmaceuticals, light manufacturing, and commercial greenhouse operations. As with the oil and gas segment, the company's public disclosures have consistently withheld specific customer names at the individual account level; filings reference customer categories and geographies rather than named counterparties. The California market, given the state's elevated electricity rates and regulatory support for distributed generation under SGIP (the Self-Generation Incentive Program), has been a persistent concentration point. Pre-bankruptcy, Capstone's 10-K filings routinely flagged that a small number of large distributor accounts — rather than end-users directly — represented a meaningful share of product revenue, meaning the company's direct visibility into the end-customer mix was itself partially mediated by the distributor channel.

Post-emergence, the shift toward Energy-as-a-Service contracting — in which Capstone Energy+ retains ownership of the generation asset and sells electrons and thermal output under a long-term offtake agreement rather than selling the hardware outright — is intended to deepen direct relationships with industrial end-users. The EaaS model improves customer stickiness and creates a recurring revenue stream, but it also requires Capstone Energy+ to carry the capital cost of the installed asset on its own balance sheet, placing demands on the post-restructuring capital structure that remain a watch item for investors.

## District Energy: Campuses, Hospitals, and Contract Longevity

University campuses and hospital complexes represent the district energy segment of Capstone's customer base. The appeal is structural: a large campus has sustained thermal and electrical loads around the clock, a long-term planning horizon that matches the economics of CHP investment, and often an explicit sustainability mandate from trustees or accreditation bodies. Hospitals add the critical requirement for resilience — uninterruptible on-site generation that can island from the grid during outages, a requirement that Capstone's microturbines satisfy in part because their fast-start capability (reaching full output in roughly 60 seconds from cold) enables them to serve as both primary generation and backup within a single asset.

The district energy segment is where Capstone's multi-unit packaged systems — combining four to six C200S units, or multiple C1000S units, in a single containerised enclosure — have found natural application. Capstone has referenced university and hospital campus deployments in general terms in IR materials but, consistent with the broader disclosure pattern, has not published a named-customer list in OTCQX-period filings reviewed within the frozen window.

## AI Data Centres: The Post-Emergence Growth Narrative

The most consequential strategic pivot in Capstone Energy+'s post-Chapter-11 positioning is the explicit targeting of AI data centre operators as a new customer category. The framing draws on a real and well-documented structural problem: hyperscalers and colocation operators expanding capacity for AI training and inference workloads are encountering utility interconnect queue times in key markets that stretch from three to seven years, according to data published by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and cited in multiple industry analyses. While waiting for utility grid capacity, data centre operators need on-site generation that can power critical loads during the ramp period — bridge power — and subsequently function as a backup or peak-shaving asset.

Capstone Energy+ IR communications have positioned the C1000S and packaged multi-megawatt configurations as suited to this application. The air-bearing architecture again provides a maintenance-cost argument: data centre operators seeking to minimise technician visits to power infrastructure in secure colocation environments find the oil-free design attractive relative to reciprocating engine gensets. The fast-start capability supports the resilience requirement. And the microturbine's low vibration profile relative to diesel gensets reduces structural load concerns in dense equipment facilities.

As of the frozen snapshot date of 2026-05-23, Capstone Energy+ had not announced a publicly named AI data centre customer in OTCQX filings or press releases reviewed for this dossier. The pipeline commentary in management communications has been directional rather than contractual. This is a material disclosure gap: the AI data centre narrative is the primary growth vector in the company's post-emergence equity story, but the transition from pipeline engagement to signed contracts with named counterparties had not been confirmed in primary sources within the frozen window.

## The Microturbine Supply Chain

Capstone Energy+'s manufacturing footprint is concentrated at its Southern California campus, historically in Chatsworth and subsequently in Van Nuys. The company has long described a substantially vertically integrated manufacturing model for its core rotating and thermal components, which it has argued is necessary to protect proprietary tolerances in the air-bearing assembly and the recuperator.

| Component | Description | Capstone's approach |
|---|---|---|
| Air bearings | Foil-type hydrodynamic bearings; no oil lubrication; single-shaft assembly | Manufactured in-house; core IP |
| Recuperator heat exchanger | Primary surface, counterflow design; stainless steel foil construction; recovers ~75% of exhaust enthalpy | Manufactured in-house; historically a supply bottleneck at volume ramp |
| Combustor | Low-NOx lean-premixed design; natural gas, propane, associated gas, biogas, hydrogen-blend capable | In-house; combustor design is fuel-flexibility-critical |
| Power electronics / inverter | High-speed generator output rectified and inverted to grid-synchronous AC; digital control board | Partially in-house, with contract manufacturing for electronics sub-assemblies |
| Enclosure and balance-of-plant | Containerised packaging, heat recovery ducting, controls integration | Mix of in-house fabrication and outside suppliers |

The recuperator is the component that has historically created the most operational risk in Capstone's supply chain. Because the recuperator operates continuously at high temperatures and differential pressures, fatigue cracking over a multi-year operating cycle requires scheduled replacement; managing recuperator lead times and inventory has been a recurring operational challenge flagged in pre-bankruptcy filings. Post-emergence, the company has not provided granular supply chain disclosures in OTCQX-period communications, leaving the current state of recuperator inventory and supplier relationships opaque.

## Fuel Flexibility and the Associated Gas Advantage

Capstone microturbines are rated to operate on natural gas pipeline quality, low-BTU associated gas, biogas from landfill and wastewater sources, propane, diesel, and hydrogen blends up to concentrations disclosed in product specification sheets. This fuel flexibility is operationally significant across all three of the company's established customer segments and underlies the emerging data centre application as well.

At upstream oil and gas sites, the ability to run directly on wet associated gas — without the methane separation and pressure conditioning that some competing technologies require — reduces balance-of-plant cost and simplifies permitting. At landfill and wastewater treatment facilities, biogas utilisation satisfies both the economics of cheap fuel and the regulatory incentive structures for renewable generation. At district energy customers with sustainability mandates, the hydrogen blend capability — currently tested to concentrations disclosed in Capstone product literature — provides a credible pathway to lower lifecycle carbon intensity as hydrogen supply infrastructure matures.

For the AI data centre application, the primary fuel is expected to be pipeline natural gas at sites with adequate gas utility service, with the microturbine positioned as lower-emission than diesel backup generation and as dispatchable in a way that solar-plus-storage configurations cannot replicate across multi-day weather events. The bridge-power narrative hinges on this dispatchability argument, and it is the most technically defensible element of Capstone Energy+'s AI data centre pitch — regardless of whether the pipeline has yet converted to signed revenue.

chapters.title: Where Capstone Energy+ sits against Bloom Energy, Cummins, Caterpillar, and broader distributed power
chapters.body:
## A Crowded Arena with Fragmented Technology Stacks

Distributed power generation is not a single market but a collection of overlapping niches separated by scale, fuel type, emissions tolerance, and deployment context. Capstone Energy+'s competitive position as of the spring 2026 snapshot was shaped by three structural realities: its microturbine technology occupied a narrow band of the power density spectrum where its engineering characteristics genuinely differentiated it from alternatives; the dominant installed base of distributed backup and prime power worldwide remained reciprocating engine gensets supplied at scale by Cummins, Caterpillar, and a long tail of regional assemblers; and Bloom Energy had moved aggressively into the same premium, low-emissions distributed-power segment that Capstone historically occupied, with substantially more capital, a larger installed base, and a NYSE listing that afforded it investor visibility and financing flexibility that Capstone — a small-cap OTCQX-listed post-bankruptcy company — could not match.

## The Genset Floor: Cummins and Caterpillar

Reciprocating engine gensets from Cummins (CMI) and Caterpillar (CAT) established the de facto price floor for distributed backup and prime power. Diesel and natural gas gensets from both companies could be procured for installed costs typically in the range of $300 to $600 per kilowatt at commercial and industrial scales — materially below the $1,000 to $2,000-plus per kilowatt range that industry practitioners associated with microturbine installations. That capex gap was the persistent headwind against which every microturbine vendor, including Capstone, competed. Cummins's Power Generation segment and Caterpillar's Electric Power division collectively represented a multi-billion-dollar global franchise with deep distribution networks, standardised service infrastructure, and decades of customer familiarity. Caterpillar's Solar Turbines subsidiary also competed in small industrial gas turbines at larger scales — generally above 1 MW and extending into multi-megawatt packages — a range where Capstone's C1200S and packaged multi-unit systems touched the lower edge.

The reciprocating engine's disadvantages were well-documented in distributed-generation literature. NOx emissions from natural gas reciprocating engines, absent selective catalytic reduction aftertreatment, ranged from roughly 50 to several hundred parts per million — an order of magnitude above the sub-9 ppm NOx specification Capstone claimed for its C200S and larger units under natural gas firing. In air quality non-attainment areas — the South Coast Air Quality Management District in Southern California being the most commercially significant — that emissions gap translated directly into permitting constraints that disadvantaged genset alternatives. Maintenance intervals for reciprocating engines, driven by oil and filter change cycles, typically fell between 500 and 2,000 hours; Capstone cited scheduled maintenance intervals of 8,000 hours for its units, a function of the air-bearing rotor design that eliminated liquid lubrication. Neither the emissions advantage nor the maintenance interval claim could be independently verified from Capstone's OTCQX-level public filings as of the snapshot date — the company's post-emergence financial disclosures did not publish independent benchmarking data on a comparable basis.

Generac (GNRC), primarily a residential and light-commercial backup power vendor, occupied a lower scale range and did not represent a direct competitive threat in the industrial, oil-and-gas, or data-centre segments that Capstone pursued.

## Bloom Energy: The Premium-Segment Rival

The most pointed competitive comparison for a sophisticated distributed-power investor was with Bloom Energy (BE), the San Jose-based solid-oxide fuel cell manufacturer. Where Capstone competed on microturbine technology, Bloom deployed electrochemical energy conversion — solid-oxide fuel cells that consumed natural gas or hydrogen to produce electricity at roughly 53–65 percent electrical efficiency in fuel cell mode, materially above the 25–30 percent simple-cycle electrical efficiency of Capstone's microturbines. Bloom's Energy Servers, packaged in modular 100-kilowatt increments and typically deployed in multi-hundred-kilowatt to multi-megawatt configurations, had accumulated a substantial commercial and enterprise installed base across technology campuses, hospitals, retail chains, and, by the early 2020s, data centre operators including several hyperscalers.

Bloom's strategic pivot toward AI data centre power was explicit and well-capitalised. The company's fiscal 2024 revenues exceeded $1.3 billion, its NYSE listing gave it equity currency for growth capital, and its partnerships with hyperscaler operators were disclosed in SEC filings. Capstone's post-emergence revenue scale — not fully disclosed in accessible OTCQX filings as of the snapshot date — was categorically smaller; the disclosure gap here is material and should not be papered over. Bloom operated in a different financial weight class.

The technology comparison was not simply an efficiency table. Bloom's SOFC units required natural gas infrastructure or hydrogen supply and did not offer the same tolerance for degraded-quality or variable-composition fuel streams that made Capstone microturbines commercially interesting in oil-and-gas flare-gas recovery. Capstone's fuel flexibility — documented across natural gas, propane, liquefied petroleum gas, flare or associated gas, biogas, digester gas, and hydrogen blends — was a specific engineering characteristic that SOFC technology replicated less cleanly at the lower-quality end of the fuel spectrum. In oil and gas upstream applications where associated gas composition could vary substantially by field, the microturbine's tolerance for fuel variability was a genuine differentiator.

## Japanese and International Microturbine Alternatives

Within the narrower microturbine sub-segment, Capstone's competitive set was thin. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Kawasaki Heavy Industries, and IHI Corporation each maintained small gas turbine and microturbine programs, but their commercial focus in distributed generation sat at larger scales and served primarily domestic Japanese industrial and utility markets. No Japanese vendor had established a material competing commercial footprint against Capstone in North America or the oil-and-gas-facing international markets that historically comprised Capstone's distribution network. European microturbine vendors, including earlier-stage development-stage companies, had not achieved the installed base or product range breadth that Capstone had accumulated over three decades. As of the snapshot date, Capstone appeared to retain meaningful position as the largest volume commercial microturbine manufacturer in the Western Hemisphere, though that position reflected a thin competitive field rather than a robust moat.

## The EaaS Contracting Layer

Capstone's post-emergence strategic communications emphasised the Energy-as-a-Service model as a competitive differentiator distinct from its technology characteristics. The EaaS structure — in which Capstone or its distribution partners retained equipment ownership and charged customers on a per-kilowatt-hour or service-fee basis — reduced customer upfront capital commitment and shifted the capex gap relative to genset alternatives into an operating-cost comparison. Bloom Energy had long operated a similar model through its Power Purchase Agreement and managed-services offerings; Cummins and Caterpillar sold equipment through dealers and did not historically operate at-scale EaaS structures comparable to fuel cell or microturbine vendors.

Whether Capstone's EaaS pipeline had converted into a durable recurring revenue base by the snapshot date could not be determined from available public disclosures. OTCQX reporting requirements are materially less demanding than those governing NASDAQ or NYSE-listed companies; Capstone's CGEH filings did not disclose contracted EaaS backlog, customer concentration, or revenue composition with the granularity available from Bloom's 10-K filings.

## The Data Centre Positioning Problem

| Vendor | Technology | Typical installed cost/kW | NOx emissions | Fuel flexibility | Data centre deployment evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cummins / CAT gensets | Reciprocating engine | ~$300–$600 | High (50–500+ ppm) | Diesel, nat gas | Widespread (standard backup) |
| Bloom Energy | Solid-oxide fuel cell | ~$5,000–$8,000+ | Very low | Nat gas, H₂ | Disclosed hyperscaler partnerships |
| Capstone Energy+ | Microturbine | ~$1,000–$2,000+ | Ultra-low (<9 ppm) | Broad fuel range | Cited as target; no disclosed deployments as of snapshot |

The AI data centre bridge-power opportunity created a specific competitive intersection. Hyperscaler operators facing utility interconnect queue delays of five to ten years in constrained markets needed dispatchable on-site generation that could be deployed in weeks rather than years. Diesel gensets remained the default solution — fast to source, widely available, financeable — but faced NOx and particulate emissions constraints that complicated air permitting in California, the Pacific Northwest, and Northern Virginia data centre corridors. Microturbines' emissions profile was therefore a structural advantage in those specific geographies. Capstone's management communications highlighted this positioning explicitly in post-emergence investor materials.

The competitive risk was straightforward: Bloom Energy was better-capitalised, had existing data centre customer relationships, and operated at power densities more suited to the multi-megawatt blocks that hyperscalers typically specified. Capstone's C1200S and packaged multi-unit systems could aggregate to several megawatts, but the project execution capability of a post-bankruptcy small-cap company competing for hyperscaler contracts alongside Bloom's commercial organisation represented an execution gap that public disclosures did not resolve. As of the snapshot date, no Capstone Energy+ data centre deployment had been publicly disclosed with the specificity — customer name, power capacity, contract structure — that would allow an investor to assess whether the strategic positioning had translated into commercial traction.

chapters.title: From 2000 IPO through Capstone Green Energy rebrand, Chapter 11, and AI data centre opportunity
chapters.body:
## The Long Road from Van Nuys to NASDAQ

Capstone Turbine Corporation was incorporated in 1988 in Van Nuys, California, its founders betting that the air-bearing microturbine — a compact gas turbine running on a thin film of pressurised air rather than oil, with a single moving part rotating at speeds exceeding 90,000 revolutions per minute — could disrupt distributed power generation for industrial and commercial customers. The technology proposition was compelling on paper: near-zero oil maintenance, fuel flexibility spanning natural gas, propane, diesel, flared landfill gas and associated petroleum gas, ultra-low NOx emissions, and modular scalability from a 30-kilowatt C30 through packaged multi-megawatt configurations combining multiple C1000S and C1200S units behind a common control system.

By the late 1990s, Capstone had attracted sufficient institutional interest to pursue a public listing.

## The 2000 NASDAQ IPO and Its Structural Trap

Capstone Turbine Corporation completed its initial public offering on the NASDAQ in 2000, raising capital during the height of the clean-energy enthusiasm that accompanied the broader technology bubble. The timing proved as much curse as opportunity. The subsequent market correction exposed the company's structural challenge: a technically mature product addressing a genuine industrial need, but facing long project sales cycles, capital-intensive manufacturing, and lumpy equipment-delivery revenue that resisted the smooth recurring curves institutional equity investors required.

The oil and gas sector — upstream operators seeking to monetise flared associated gas at well sites, midstream processors running prime power at compression stations — remained Capstone's most durable revenue source across the two decades that followed. Combined heat and power installations at university campuses, hospital complexes, hotels, and broader district-energy applications provided a second demand pillar. Neither segment delivered the volume ramp that could lift the company to consistent profitability.

| Fiscal Year (ending March 31) | Revenue (USD millions) |
|---|---|
| FY2020 | ~$75M |
| FY2021 | ~$73M |
| FY2022 | ~$95M |
| FY2023 | ~$77M |

*Source: Capstone Green Energy pre-Chapter-11 NASDAQ disclosures. FY2024 and subsequent figures reflect materially reduced post-emergence OTCQX reporting cadence.*

Operating losses were a persistent feature across virtually every fiscal year of the NASDAQ tenure despite the revenue base. The capital structure absorbed repeated equity dilutions as the company funded operations through secondary offerings and revolving credit facilities. The FY2022 peak of approximately $95 million — representing the highest revenue in the company's publicly listed history — was followed by a decline to $77 million in FY2023, as post-pandemic supply chain disruptions and lumpy project timing combined with the operational costs of a strategic transition already underway.

## The 2021 Rebrand: Capstone Green Energy

In 2021, under chief executive Darren Jamison — who had led the company since the mid-2000s — Capstone Turbine Corporation rebranded as Capstone Green Energy Corporation. The name change was more than cosmetic. It reflected a deliberate pivot toward integrated Energy-as-a-Service contracting, in which Capstone would own and operate microgrid assets on customer premises under long-term power purchase or service agreements, rather than simply selling turbine hardware on a project basis.

The EaaS model carried a familiar appeal to anyone who had followed the SaaS transition in software: predictable recurring revenues, deeper customer relationships, and a valuation premium over pure equipment manufacturing. It also introduced balance-sheet complexity, requiring Capstone to finance asset ownership across an income statement that had never generated sustained operating profit. The green energy positioning simultaneously aligned the company with the accelerating ESG capital flows of the early 2020s. Capstone's microturbines could run on biogas, landfill gas, and anaerobic digester gas — genuinely lower-carbon fuels — providing a credible sustainability narrative alongside the industrial efficiency story.

## The Road to Chapter 11

By the fiscal year ending March 2023, revenue had retreated to approximately $77 million from the prior-year peak. The combination of post-pandemic supply chain stress, customer project delays across the oil and gas sector, and the working-capital demands of the EaaS transition pressed on the company's liquidity. Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group, by then the principal secured creditor, held significant leverage over the capital structure.

On September 28, 2023, Capstone Green Energy Holdings filed for Chapter 11 protection in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware. The filing was structured as a prepackaged restructuring — meaning the substantive terms had been negotiated with principal creditors prior to the court process, enabling an accelerated timeline through the proceedings. Pre-petition common equity was thereby substantially extinguished, consistent with standard prepackaged restructuring outcomes when enterprise value sits below the senior creditor waterline.

The prepackaged structure delivered the speed its architects intended. On December 7, 2023 — fewer than eleven weeks after the initial filing — Capstone emerged from Chapter 11 with a restructured balance sheet and reorganised equity ownership concentrated among former Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending and other pre-petition creditors. Darren Jamison did not continue as chief executive into the post-emergence entity. The leadership transition was part of the broader operational reset that accompanied the balance-sheet restructuring. Confirmation of the post-emergence executive team requires verification against current OTCQX governance disclosures and Capstone Energy+ IR communications, given the reduced reporting cadence of the post-emergence entity.

## Capstone Energy+: The Post-Emergence Identity

The company subsequently rebranded from Capstone Green Energy to Capstone Energy+ Inc, a name carrying both the legacy of the Capstone microturbine franchise and a forward posture toward broader energy solutions. Shares traded on the OTCQX market under the ticker CGEH — a materially different venue from the NASDAQ listing of the prior two decades, reflecting the reduced scale and altered investor base of the restructured entity.

Public disclosure declined commensurately. OTCQX reporting requirements are substantially less prescriptive than NASDAQ equivalents, and the post-emergence financial statements available through the May 2026 snapshot reflected this reduced transparency. Investors following CGEH were working with materially less granular disclosure than the pre-Chapter-11 entity had provided — a reality that sophisticated participants in small-cap restructured equities will recognise, and that represents a standing analytical handicap throughout any assessment of the post-emergence operating trajectory.

## The AI Data Centre Bridge-Power Thesis

Against this restructuring backdrop, a new demand signal was emerging that Capstone's post-emergence strategic communications identified as a material forward catalyst: the AI data centre bridge-power opportunity.

The proximate driver was the unprecedented surge in grid interconnection demand generated by hyperscale AI infrastructure buildout. Data centre operators — from the major hyperscalers to the expanding class of colocation and wholesale providers building AI-optimised campuses — encountered utility interconnection queues stretching from eighteen months to several years across high-demand markets in the United States. For an industry calibrated to tight timelines between site selection and commissioning, the utility queue backlog represented a genuine constraint on revenue-generating deployment.

Capstone's microturbines addressed this constraint directly. The C1000S and C1200S units — capable of 1 megawatt and 1.2 megawatt output respectively, and parallelable in multi-unit configurations to double-digit megawatt deployments — could be sited, installed, and commissioned on a fraction of the lead time required for permanent utility interconnection. Natural gas supply, typically available at industrial sites well ahead of full utility power delivery, provided the fuel. The EaaS contracting structure Capstone had been developing since 2021 was well-suited to the application: a data centre operator with constrained capital expenditure budgets during construction could take turbine capacity on an operating lease or power purchase agreement, paying for availability rather than owning the hardware.

As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, Capstone Energy+ had communicated the AI data centre opportunity prominently in forward-looking materials. The pipeline conversion rate — the translation of identified opportunity into contracted EaaS revenue with named counterparties — remained a material disclosure gap, consistent with the reduced reporting cadence of the OTCQX listing. The catalysts that would determine whether the post-Chapter-11 positioning translated into sustained operating performance were therefore clear in structure if not yet in magnitude: the pace of AI data centre EaaS contract announcements; the post-emergence revenue trajectory relative to the approximately $77 million pre-filing run rate; and the operating leverage that a restructured, lower-overhead balance sheet might finally allow to flow through to an income statement that had resisted profitability across a quarter-century of public company life.

chapters.title: Microturbine technology, air-bearing IP, and the EaaS platform
chapters.body:
## An Architecture Built Around One Moving Part

The engineering proposition at the heart of Capstone Energy+'s franchise is deceptively simple: a microturbine that achieves reliable, low-maintenance distributed power generation by eliminating the components most likely to fail. Where a conventional reciprocating generator demands regular oil changes, coolant management, and periodic overhaul of pistons, valves, and crankshaft bearings, a Capstone microturbine operates on a single rotating assembly — compressor, turbine wheel, and permanent-magnet generator mounted on one common shaft — supported entirely by air bearings and requiring no lubricating oil whatsoever.

That air-bearing architecture, developed and refined across more than three decades since the company's 1988 founding, remains the most defensible element of the technology platform. Conventional hydrodynamic or rolling-element bearings require pressurised oil systems, oil coolers, filtration hardware, and scheduled oil changes; in remote or unmanned deployments — oil field wellpads, offshore platforms, data centre generator rooms — that maintenance burden is both costly and operationally risky. Capstone's air-bearing journals use a thin pressurised film of process air rather than oil, sustaining the rotor at operating speed without any lubricated contact between moving surfaces. The design does not merely reduce maintenance intervals; it changes the maintenance paradigm entirely.

The rotor assembly operates at approximately 96,000 revolutions per minute — far above the synchronous frequencies usable by the grid — meaning the turbine's raw AC output cannot be connected directly to utility infrastructure or building loads. Capstone's power electronics package, integrated into each turbine unit, first rectifies the high-frequency AC to DC and then inverts it to a clean 50 or 60 Hz output. This digital power electronics layer, often overlooked in assessments of the microturbine IP, is a significant barrier to replication: the control algorithms governing inverter switching, load tracking, and grid synchronisation represent decades of field-calibrated development.

## The Recuperator and the Efficiency Case

Raw thermodynamic efficiency from a simple-cycle small gas turbine is modest — typically well below 20 percent for the machine sizes Capstone produces. The recuperator addresses this structural penalty by recovering heat from the turbine exhaust stream and using it to pre-heat compressed air before it enters the combustor. In Capstone's design, the recuperator is a compact annular heat exchanger wrapped around the turbine core; according to published technical data, it raises electrical efficiency into the 25–33 percent range depending on load and ambient conditions, materially closing the gap with larger turbine classes on a per-kWh basis.

When combined heat and power operation is configured — routing residual exhaust thermal energy to process heat, space heating, or absorption cooling — overall system efficiency climbs further. In cogeneration applications, the thermal product that would otherwise exhaust to atmosphere becomes a revenue-contributing output, which is precisely the economics that made Capstone equipment attractive to district energy operators, hospitals, and university campuses over two decades of deployment before the 2023 restructuring.

## Fuel Flexibility as Competitive IP

A recurring theme in Capstone's commercial positioning, and one that became more commercially salient as the company pivoted toward oil-and-gas field applications, is the machine's ability to operate on fuel streams that would damage or destroy a conventional reciprocating engine. Natural gas is the baseline; beyond that, published Capstone specifications cover biogas with methane content as low as 35 percent, associated petroleum gas that would otherwise be flared at the wellhead, landfill gas, digester gas, and — in more recent R&D disclosures — hydrogen blends.

The combustor design is central to this flexibility. Capstone's annular, lean-premixed combustor operates at lower peak temperatures than conventional gas turbines, which suppresses nitrogen-oxide formation and also reduces the thermal shock risks that make high-hydrogen fuels problematic for older combustor metallurgy. The company has published test data on blended hydrogen operation, though the precise percentage blends demonstrated under commercial field conditions have not been fully disclosed in OTCQX filings available as of the snapshot date. The hydrogen positioning represents an important strategic optionality claim for the post-emergence business — AI data centre operators and industrial customers evaluating long-term fuel supply risk are increasingly attentive to hydrogen-readiness — but the depth of that IP relative to purpose-built hydrogen power systems remains an acknowledged disclosure gap.

## The EaaS Software Layer

Energy-as-a-Service, as Capstone frames it, is not simply a financing structure. The company built a remote monitoring and fleet management platform — historically called the Capstone Remote Monitoring System — that aggregates real-time telemetry from deployed units into a centralised operations environment. Sensor data covering turbine inlet temperature, exhaust temperature, power output, fuel consumption, bearing air pressure, and dozens of additional parameters flow continuously from field units to Capstone's operations centre, enabling predictive maintenance interventions before faults develop into unplanned outages.

For a customer contracting under an EaaS arrangement — paying a fixed dollar-per-kWh or dollar-per-kWh-plus-thermal rate rather than purchasing hardware outright — the operational uptime guarantee that Capstone underwrites depends entirely on that monitoring infrastructure. The software layer is therefore not a value-added overlay but a load-bearing component of the EaaS business model. Capstone has described the monitoring system as proprietary, though granular disclosure on the underlying software architecture, API integrations with third-party SCADA or building management systems, or cybersecurity certification status was not available in public filings reviewed through the snapshot date.

## Patent Position and Portfolio Depth

Capstone's cumulative patent position spans several hundred issued patents across the United States and key international jurisdictions, accumulated over more than thirty years of microturbine development. The portfolio covers air-bearing design variants, recuperator geometries, combustor configurations, power electronics topologies, and control software methodologies. The age of the portfolio is itself a double-edged characteristic: issued patents on foundational air-bearing designs filed in the 1990s have largely expired, leaving those specific claim scopes in the public domain, while more recent filings on hydrogen-blend combustion, advanced recuperator materials, and EaaS software controls remain in-force and commercially relevant.

No competitor has successfully replicated the air-bearing microturbine design at commercial scale — Ingersoll Rand's discontinued PowerWorks product and Elliott Energy Systems' earlier turbine program both exited the market without establishing durable franchises — suggesting that the accumulated manufacturing know-how, field reliability data, and software calibration embedded in Capstone's platform constitutes a form of tacit IP that supplements the formal patent estate.

chapters.title: Post-Chapter-11 execution, AI demand conversion, competitive intensity, capital structure
chapters.body:
## Post-Chapter-11 Operational Execution

The most proximate risk facing any investor in Capstone Energy+ is the simplest: the company emerged from Chapter 11 in December 2023 as a materially smaller, privately re-owned, OTCQX-listed entity operating under reduced public reporting obligations. Pre-emergence, Capstone Turbine had been a NASDAQ-listed company since 2000; the transition to OTCQX eliminated quarterly earnings calls and the depth of SEC disclosure typical of exchange-listed issuers, and reduced the frequency and granularity of financial reporting available to outside investors.

The restructuring installed reorganised creditors — Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending Group plus other former lenders — as the dominant equity holders, replacing a diffuse retail and institutional shareholder base. That ownership transition is a common feature of prepackaged Chapter 11 outcomes. What creates analytical difficulty is the resulting disclosure gap: confirmed post-emergence revenue, gross margin, and cash-burn data for fiscal year 2024 (ending March 2024) and beyond were not available in primary OTCQX filings through the snapshot date of May 23, 2026. Investors evaluating Capstone Energy+ are operating with meaningfully less visibility than they would have with a NASDAQ or NYSE comparable at equivalent revenue scale.

The operational execution risk compounds this. Pre-Chapter-11, Capstone Turbine produced roughly $75–95 million in annual revenue across fiscal years 2020–2023 but never achieved sustained profitability across its multi-decade public history. The Chapter 11 filing reflected not only balance-sheet distress but operational scaling challenges and customer-receivable concerns — structural issues that balance-sheet restructuring alone does not resolve.

**Mitigants:** The prepackaged structure kept the core microturbine engineering and manufacturing operations intact. Operational rightsizing through the restructuring may improve unit economics even if top-line growth is slower. **Residual concern:** Without audited post-emergence financials publicly available, the execution improvement thesis remains unverified.

---

## AI Data Centre Opportunity Conversion

Post-emergence communications from Capstone Energy+ have prominently emphasised the AI data centre backup-and-bridge power opportunity. The strategic logic is coherent: utility interconnect queues in major data centre markets — Northern Virginia, Phoenix, Chicago, Dallas — had lengthened substantially by 2024 and 2025, prompting hyperscale operators and colocation providers to evaluate on-site dispatchable generation as a bridge while grid connections were secured. Microturbines offer low-emissions, multi-fuel-capable, modular power in precisely the size bands relevant to incremental data centre capacity.

The risk is that the opportunity had remained, through the snapshot date, at the level of strategic communication rather than confirmed contractual conversion. No specific AI data centre customer contract — customer identity, contracted capacity, revenue terms — had been disclosed in primary OTCQX filings or IR releases reviewed through May 23, 2026. The category is described as "emerging" in the company's own strategic-posture language. That disclosure gap leaves investors unable to assess whether AI data centre revenue was a material contributor to post-emergence results or remained a pipeline-stage aspiration.

**Mitigants:** The underlying demand driver — utility interconnect scarcity — was real and independently documented. Capstone's packaged microgrid configurations are technically suited to the bridge-power application. **Residual concern:** Technology suitability and market demand do not guarantee commercial conversion. Without disclosed contracts, AI data centre revenue cannot be modelled with any precision.

---

## Competitive Intensity

Capstone Energy+ competes against well-capitalised, investment-grade incumbents with substantially greater balance-sheet and distribution capacity.

| Competitor | Primary technology | Listing | Competitive position |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bloom Energy | Solid-oxide fuel cells | NASDAQ | Data centre and industrial CHP; disclosed hyperscaler deployments |
| Cummins | Diesel and gas reciprocating gensets | NYSE | Global genset market leader; massive service network |
| Caterpillar Power | Diesel and gas reciprocating gensets | NYSE | Global genset and UPS market; investment-grade balance sheet |

Bloom Energy is the most direct competitive analogue for the AI data centre application, offering high-efficiency stationary fuel cells with an established hyperscaler customer reference list that no OTCQX-scale entity has matched in disclosed terms. Cummins and Caterpillar compete on reciprocating gas gensets — lower capital cost and widely available, lacking the microturbine's emissions profile but benefitting from a global installed base and service network that confer decisive procurement advantages.

Capstone Energy+'s differentiated position rests on microturbine-specific attributes: fewer moving parts than reciprocating engines, air-bearing technology that eliminates liquid lubrication, multi-fuel capability, and a low-emissions profile that matters in jurisdictions with air-quality permitting constraints. These attributes have sustained commercial demand for three decades. They have not translated into durable profitability against the competitive backdrop described above. **Residual concern:** Bloom Energy's balance sheet and disclosed hyperscaler relationships represent a formidable position in the specific segment Capstone Energy+ has targeted. A small-cap OTCQX entity competing for large data centre procurement decisions against investment-grade vendors faces structural disadvantages.

---

## Capital Structure Adequacy

The prepackaged restructuring eliminated the pre-emergence debt burden and installed a new equity ownership group. The post-emergence capital structure — available liquidity, any remaining debt facilities, cash runway against operating burn — had not been publicly disclosed in sufficient granularity through the snapshot date. This is a material gap for any investor attempting to assess solvency risk in a post-restructuring small-cap.

Pre-Chapter-11, Capstone Turbine had a persistent history of operating cash outflows against a revenue base that never generated durable free cash flow. Whether the post-emergence entity had resolved the structural cash consumption issue through cost reduction, or whether it retained a capital-dependent operating model requiring periodic equity or debt raises, could not be determined from available primary disclosure. **Residual concern:** The risk of a dilutive secondary capital raise, or further covenant pressure from any remaining lender facilities, cannot be assessed given the disclosure gap.

---

## Customer Concentration

Capstone Turbine's pre-Chapter-11 revenue was historically concentrated in oil and gas and industrial CHP applications, with a material share routed through a small number of authorised distributors. Customer concentration — dependence on a limited number of end-users or channel partners — was a disclosed risk factor in pre-emergence SEC filings. Post-emergence, the concentration question persists: the shift toward EaaS contracting could reduce or increase concentration depending on whether EaaS contracts are signed with a diversified customer set or a handful of anchor counterparties. No post-emergence concentration disclosure was available through the snapshot date.

---

## Fuel Price Exposure

Capstone microturbines operate primarily on natural gas, with multi-fuel capability extending to propane, flare gas, and biogas. Revenue exposure to natural gas price volatility is indirect — Capstone sells and services equipment and does not typically take commodity price risk on the fuel itself. EaaS contract structures, however, where Capstone may retain responsibility for energy delivery economics, create potential pass-through exposure depending on contract terms. The EaaS model's economics are materially sensitive to the spread between gas input cost and the contracted energy delivery price. No EaaS contract terms had been disclosed publicly through the snapshot date, leaving fuel-price pass-through risk unquantified.

---

## Cross-Cutting: OTCQX Liquidity and Reporting Cadence

The migration from NASDAQ to OTCQX post-emergence is consequential across every risk category catalogued here. OTCQX-listed issuers are not subject to SEC periodic reporting obligations at the frequency or depth required of exchange-listed companies. Bid-ask spreads are typically wider than NASDAQ comparables; institutional participation is lower; and the secondary-market liquidity available to an investor seeking to exit a position may be materially constrained relative to what the pre-emergence listing offered. For a sophisticated investor evaluating Capstone Energy+ as a post-restructuring turnaround, the OTCQX structure means that the standard diligence toolkit — quarterly earnings, 10-K/10-Q SEC filings, earnings call transcripts, sell-side coverage — is partially or wholly unavailable. Each of the six risks above carries a higher residual uncertainty as a direct consequence of that reduced disclosure environment, and that structural feature should be treated as a standalone risk rather than merely a disclosure inconvenience.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## A thin consensus, a crowded opportunity, and the gap between them

The first honest constraint any investor must accept when building a 12-month forward view on Capstone Energy+ is structural: the company does not carry sell-side coverage in the conventional sense. OTCQX reporting obligations are materially lighter than NYSE or NASDAQ equivalents — no mandatory quarterly 10-Q filing cycle, a narrower set of institutional eyes on each disclosure, and a management communications cadence calibrated to a post-emergence company still establishing its rhythm with the capital markets. There is, at the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, no published Street consensus for CGEH revenue, EBITDA, or earnings per share. Any forward estimate framework must be constructed bottom-up from management commentary, disclosed backlog, and observable market dynamics. That caveat acknowledged, the setup is meaningfully asymmetric — and the next twelve months should provide the first real evidence of whether the post-Chapter-11 thesis is converting.

## Fiscal calendar and the catalyst sequence

Capstone Energy+ reports on a fiscal year ending in March. From the May 2026 snapshot date, the forward calendar runs through four quarters: Q1 FY2027 closing June 2026, Q2 closing September 2026, Q3 closing December 2026, and Q4 closing March 2027. The company's full fiscal year 2026 — the first complete fiscal year under the post-emergence structure — likely closed March 2026 and should be disclosed by mid-summer 2026. That FY2026 annual disclosure is arguably the most important single data point in the next twelve months: it will establish the post-emergence revenue baseline against which all forward growth claims can be calibrated.

**June–July 2026 — FY2026 annual disclosure.** This is the first catalyst in the sequence and the one carrying the greatest informational weight. Prior to the Chapter 11 filing, the last fully-public fiscal year (FY2023 ending March 2023) produced approximately $77 million in revenue. The post-emergence period brought operational restructuring, a strategic pivot toward Energy-as-a-Service contracting, and — critically — a new customer vertical in AI data centre backup and bridge power. Whether the post-emergence revenue run rate held near the pre-filing level, contracted as legacy product-sale volume was de-emphasised, or grew via EaaS contract additions is not publicly confirmed as of the frozen snapshot. The FY2026 disclosure will answer that question and provide the first audited view of the post-emergence balance sheet, cash generation profile, and backlog.

**September 2026 — Q1 FY2027 interim update.** The EaaS model converts installed-base capex into contracted recurring revenue streams. The Q1 update will be the first quarterly data point against the newly-established FY2026 baseline. Investors should look for sequential EaaS contract count growth and any commentary on AI data centre pipeline conversion from prospect to signed contract.

**October–November 2026 — potential AI data centre design-win announcements.** The broader AI infrastructure buildout is producing a wave of data centre operator interest in on-site dispatchable generation given utility interconnect queue tightening across Northern Virginia, Silicon Valley, Texas, and increasingly secondary markets. Capstone's management has positioned the company's microturbine configurations — particularly the C600S, C1000S, and packaged multi-megawatt systems — as suited to the bridge-power application: dispatchable, low-noise-signature, capable of running on natural gas or alternative fuels, and deployable faster than utility-scale grid interconnects clear the queue. A named data centre design win in Q2 FY2027 would materially re-rate the forward revenue expectations.

**December 2026 — Q2 FY2027 interim update.** The December quarter update will carry the first full read on whether the AI data centre vertical is contributing measurable revenue or remains in the pipeline-building phase. It will also provide a midpoint view on whether EaaS backlog is growing fast enough to offset any legacy product-sale volume churn.

**March 2027 — fiscal year end.** Full FY2027 close, with the forward model beginning to develop a two-year earnings history under the post-emergence structure.

## The estimates framework: bottom-up in the absence of consensus

Because no published Street consensus exists, a rigorous forward model requires explicit bottom-up assumptions. The framework below is constructed from disclosed pre-filing revenue history, observable market dynamics, and the EaaS contracting model's revenue recognition mechanics.

| Period | Revenue estimate (USD M) | Key assumption |
|---|---|---|
| FY2026 (ended March 2026) | 65–80 | Post-emergence operational reset; EaaS build-out offset against legacy product revenue pressure |
| Q1 FY2027 (June 2026) | 17–21 | Seasonal patterns consistent with prior years; EaaS base grows modestly |
| Q2 FY2027 (September 2026) | 18–23 | First AI data centre contribution possible if design-win pipeline converts |
| Q3 FY2027 (December 2026) | 19–25 | EaaS recurring revenue compounding; potential step-up if AI vertical materialises |
| Q4 FY2027 (March 2027) | 20–27 | Full-year EaaS growth momentum plus AI data centre delivery cycle |
| **FY2027 full year** | **74–96** | **Implies flat to +20% growth over the FY2026 baseline, driven by EaaS conversion and AI vertical** |

These ranges carry wide uncertainty bands that reflect the disclosure gap. On operating profitability: Capstone Turbine carried persistent operating losses through its pre-filing public life. The EaaS model, if successfully scaled, should improve the gross margin profile relative to pure equipment sales — contracted recurring revenue with higher visibility than lumpy project-sale quarters. Whether the post-emergence cost structure supports positive operating income within the 12-month forward window is not publicly confirmed, and the conservative base case does not assume breakeven by March 2027.

## The specific variables to track each quarter

**EaaS contract count and total contracted megawatt-hours.** The single most important metric for the bull thesis. EaaS converts the installed base into a recurring revenue stream; the growth rate of signed contracts and aggregate contracted capacity should be disclosed in any substantive management commentary. A declining or stagnant contract count would be a material negative signal.

**AI data centre pipeline and conversion.** Management has framed the AI data centre backup-and-bridge power opportunity as a meaningful incremental vertical. Investors should track: named customer wins (even redacted), MW capacity under discussion versus signed, and any indication of delivery timelines. The hyperscaler procurement cycle is long, but initial design-win announcements typically precede revenue by 9–18 months.

**Gross margin.** Pre-filing gross margins were variable and often compressed in quarters with heavy warranty or parts costs. EaaS conversion should structurally improve margin visibility. A sequential improvement in gross margin percentage would confirm the model is working.

**Cash and liquidity position.** Post-emergence, the restructured balance sheet eliminated the Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending overhang, but the company is not yet confirmed cash-generative. Liquidity runway against the forward investment requirements of the AI data centre vertical is a critical monitoring point.

**Backlog.** Any disclosed backlog figure — defined as signed contracts not yet recognised as revenue — would be the most direct leading indicator of forward revenue momentum.

## Beat versus miss: the asymmetry at the snapshot date

A beat against the framework above requires two conditions: EaaS contract count growth at a double-digit sequential pace, and at least one publicly confirmed AI data centre design win by the end of Q2 FY2027. If both materialise, the upper end of the FY2027 revenue range becomes defensible, and the operating leverage implied by a higher EaaS mix could produce the first positive operating income quarter in the company's post-emergence history. That combination — top-line re-acceleration plus operating profit inflection — would be a significant re-rating catalyst for a stock that carries no active sell-side sponsorship.

A miss looks like one of two things: either the AI data centre pipeline remains in early-stage commercial discussion through December 2026 with no signed revenue-stage contracts, or EaaS renewal and new-contract additions are offset by legacy product-sale attrition, producing flat-to-down revenue versus the prior fiscal year. The miss scenario does not require catastrophic execution failure — merely the continuation of the post-Chapter-11 cadence without visible inflection. For an OTCQX-listed company with limited institutional sponsorship, flat-or-down revenue into FY2027 and no marquee customer announcements would likely produce further equity illiquidity.

## The bull and bear setup

The bull case rests on timing asymmetry: the AI data centre buildout is creating a genuine, multi-year demand surge for dispatchable on-site power that Capstone's microturbine and EaaS integration capability is technically positioned to serve. Utility interconnect queues across the major data centre markets are measured in years. If Capstone secures even a handful of data centre operator contracts in the 2–5 MW range, the revenue contribution at post-emergence scale is material. Against a FY2026 baseline estimated at $65–80 million, a $10–15 million incremental AI data centre vertical would represent 15–20% top-line growth from a single new customer category.

The bear case is more prosaic. Capstone has spent nearly three decades building microturbine technology without ever achieving sustained profitability. The Chapter 11 process resolved the balance sheet problem but did not resolve the competitive positioning problem: Cummins, Caterpillar, and Generac all field credible large-genset and distributed generation products with far greater service network density, customer relationships, and manufacturing scale. Bloom Energy addresses the stationary fuel cell segment with a more differentiated technology story and active institutional coverage. In the AI data centre vertical specifically, the speed-to-deployment advantage Capstone cites is real but narrow — diesel genset alternatives are faster to procure and already embedded in data centre engineering standards. The bear case is not that Capstone's technology doesn't work; it is that the competitive window for the AI data centre opportunity is narrower than management's forward positioning implies, and that the EaaS conversion timeline stretches beyond what the current liquidity position can comfortably absorb.

The asymmetry at the 23 May 2026 snapshot is unusual for a company this size: the upside from confirmed AI data centre traction is large relative to the current valuation base, while the downside from continued status-quo execution is bounded by the post-emergence balance sheet restructuring. The next twelve months will determine which of those two paths is actually open.

chapters.title: AI data centre bridge-power scaling, EaaS conversion, and the 2026-2028 horizon
chapters.body:
## The utility interconnect bottleneck as structural tailwind

The AI infrastructure buildout that accelerated through 2024 and 2025 produced an uncomfortable reality for hyperscale and colocation operators alike: the United States electrical grid could not absorb new data centre load on any timeline consistent with hyperscaler deployment schedules. Utility interconnect queues in key data centre markets — Northern Virginia, Phoenix, Chicago, Dallas — stretched to between five and seven years in several major utility service territories, according to coverage by Bloomberg and Power Magazine. The consequence was not merely inconvenience. It was a structural bottleneck that, for the first time in the data centre sector's history, made on-site dispatchable generation an operational necessity rather than a reliability hedge.

Capstone Energy+'s post-emergence leadership framed this dynamic as the company's most material near-term opportunity. The microturbine configurations most relevant to the data centre application — the C200S at 200 kilowatts, the C1000S signature series at one megawatt, and the C1200S at 1.2 megawatts — could be stacked into packaged systems delivering several megawatts, sufficient to bridge a mid-size data centre pod while utility interconnect proceedings ran their course. The microturbine's fuel flexibility, capable of operating on pipeline natural gas, biogas, or associated flare gas, offered an additional advantage over diesel gensets in jurisdictions facing tightening air quality requirements.

The extent to which that opportunity had converted to signed contracts and booked revenue as of late May 2026, however, remained constrained by Capstone Energy+'s disclosure posture. The company's OTCQX listing under the ticker CGEH carried materially lighter reporting requirements than its predecessor Capstone Turbine Corporation's NASDAQ listing, and the post-emergence entity had not, within the scope of public filings and investor relations communications reviewed for this dossier, disclosed a named data centre customer or a specific megawatt pipeline figure. That gap between strategic narrative and verifiable commercial progress represented a material information asymmetry for investors evaluating the bridge-power thesis.

## EaaS conversion: the revenue model in transition

The Energy-as-a-Service contracting structure that Capstone had been building toward since the 2021 Capstone Green Energy rebrand represented a fundamental shift in how the company recognised and retained revenue. Under a traditional product-sale model, a microturbine transaction closed at shipment; under EaaS, the customer contracted for power output rather than the capital equipment, converting a lumpy one-time sale into a recurring monthly revenue stream. The economic logic for the customer was straightforward: no upfront capital outlay, a predictable operating cost, and outsourced maintenance responsibility aligned with the microturbine's design characteristic of scheduled parts replacement rather than unplanned repair.

For Capstone, the transition created near-term revenue headwinds — units deployed under EaaS contracts did not generate the same immediate top-line recognition as outright equipment sales — while building the contracted recurring revenue base that investors in distributed power platforms had increasingly rewarded. The pre-Chapter-11 revenue history illustrated the inherent volatility of the product-sale model: fiscal year 2022 revenue reached approximately $95 million before retreating to approximately $77 million in fiscal year 2023, a swing that reflected customer timing and macroeconomic conditions rather than any structural deterioration in end-market demand.

Post-emergence revenue figures for fiscal year 2024 and fiscal year 2025 were not publicly available in granular form within the sources reviewed for this dossier. Investors seeking to track EaaS conversion progress were operating with incomplete data — a structural characteristic of OTCQX-listed small-caps that warranted explicit acknowledgment rather than papering over with extrapolation.

## Legacy verticals: oil and gas and industrial CHP

While the AI data centre narrative captured the most investor attention in the post-emergence period, the core revenue base remained the oil and gas and industrial cogeneration verticals that had sustained Capstone's commercial existence across its multi-decade operating history.

The oil and gas application — deploying microturbines at upstream well sites to utilise associated gas that would otherwise be vented or flared, powering drilling operations or midstream compression — provided a relatively durable demand floor. Associated gas flaring restrictions had tightened across multiple US producing basins as well as internationally, creating ongoing regulatory pressure that translated to demand for flare-gas utilisation solutions. The microturbine's tolerance for variable fuel gas composition, which caused operational problems for conventional reciprocating engines, gave Capstone a differentiated position in this application category.

Industrial combined heat and power — deploying microturbines at manufacturing facilities, food processing plants, hospital campuses, and university district energy systems — represented the other pillar of the legacy revenue base. The economics of CHP improved materially as commercial electricity prices rose through the post-pandemic period; waste-heat recovery for process and space-heating applications raised the effective system efficiency well above the microturbine's electrical-only thermal conversion rate, improving project returns and compressing payback periods. Whether those economics had translated to accelerated order activity in the post-emergence period was, again, a question the available public disclosures did not fully answer.

## Risk register revisited

Four risk categories dominated the Capstone Energy+ investment thesis as of the May 2026 snapshot.

The first was competitive displacement. The AI data centre bridge-power opportunity attracted significantly better-capitalised participants. Bloom Energy's solid oxide fuel cell systems offered comparable emissions profiles with higher electrical efficiency and established relationships with hyperscale operators. Cummins and Caterpillar brought distribution depth, balance-sheet scale, and existing data centre installed bases that Capstone could not credibly match. Gas turbine manufacturers serving the larger end of the power spectrum had also moved to address the interconnect-delay problem. Capstone's differentiation — fuel flexibility, low-emissions combustion, compact footprint, predictable maintenance intervals — was real but not unchallenged.

| Competitor | Technology | Relevant scale | Principal data centre advantage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bloom Energy | Solid oxide fuel cell | 200 kW – multi-MW | High electrical efficiency; hyperscaler relationships |
| Cummins | Gas and diesel gensets | 250 kW – multi-MW | Distribution scale; existing installed base |
| Caterpillar | Gas and diesel gensets | 250 kW – multi-MW | Brand depth; service network; financial strength |
| Capstone Energy+ | Microturbine | 30 kW – several MW (packaged) | Fuel flexibility; low NOx; low maintenance interval |

The second risk was execution. Capstone's multi-decade history was one of technological credibility paired with persistent commercial underperformance. Revenue had never converted to sustained operating profitability across the entire public-company existence dating to the 2000 Nasdaq listing. The Chapter 11 filing was itself, in part, a verdict on the previous management structure's inability to translate a viable product into a viable business. Whether the post-emergence leadership — restructured under oversight of the Goldman Sachs Specialty Lending-led creditor group following the December 2023 emergence — had genuinely altered the operational and commercial execution model remained unverifiable from public disclosures alone.

The third risk was the OTCQX disclosure environment itself. Reduced reporting cadence meant that material developments — contract wins, EaaS penetration rates, working capital trends — might not reach the public domain on a schedule that allowed investors to position ahead of outcomes. This was a structural feature of the post-emergence entity, not a curable deficiency.

The fourth risk was capital. EaaS deployments required Capstone to fund installed equipment on its own balance sheet, creating ongoing financing requirements that a small, OTCQX-listed company with a restructured post-bankruptcy capital structure would need to service without the equity market access that a Nasdaq listing had historically, if imperfectly, provided.

## The profitability question

Capstone Turbine Corporation reported operating losses in every fiscal year from its 2000 public listing through the fiscal year ending March 2023. The technology worked. The applications were commercially real. The end markets were genuine. What consistently failed was the translation of those inputs into a business that generated more cash than it consumed.

The post-Chapter-11 period offered conditions that had not previously coexisted: a structurally reduced cost base following the prepackaged bankruptcy, an emerging AI data centre demand category large enough to move the revenue needle for a company of Capstone's scale, and an EaaS model that — if the contracted backlog was genuinely being built — would compound recurring revenue rather than requiring constant reselling of a transactional customer base.

Whether those conditions were sufficient to produce the first sustained operating profitability in Capstone Energy+'s history across the 2026-to-2028 window was the question that the available evidence could not yet answer. The strategic logic was more compelling than at any prior point in the company's history. The financial validation, as of the frozen snapshot window, remained materially incomplete.
